questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/d5be79e0c9f09b5810459bfd8a1ce88f21e2e709dff9d20d7369681ddb61a81b.png)

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $100\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=100\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=100I=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+2q=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $24\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $100\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.001\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=100\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=100I=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.001}=1000q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}+1000q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+10q=\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/6f9417fdec3a123dbb28ae87a31c6dc49e38327178e1335030b51505f5ca2cbd.png)

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $60\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.003\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=60\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=60I=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.003}=\frac{1000}{3}q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1000}{3}q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}q=\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/726e1c886236a47159bf154fc1ad6384ffc4aa89c5b3cba6b0067a70a0a773f2.png)

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $25\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=25\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=25I=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
6\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}+250q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+10q=\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/2cccb2a1edfeed0a562303053395c6599e14cbf08f9dc5e7f07a4d657755b1ae.png)

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $15\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $250\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=250\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=250I=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
15=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}+250q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{3}{50}.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, in a series RC circuit is governed by the differential equation

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+6q=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Find the steady-state charge for this circuit.

The steady-state charge is
{{field-1}} coulombs.
questions.worked_solution:
The given equation is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+6{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+6\alpha =\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{1}{12}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{12}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-6t}+\frac{1}{12}.
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}=A{e}^{-6t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The constant ${q}_{p}=\frac{1}{12}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to \infty ,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

Therefore, the steady-state charge is $\frac{1}{12}$ coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=60\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=60I=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}.

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.003}=\frac{1000}{3}q.

$$
18=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1000}{3}q,
$$

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}q=\frac{3}{10}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}{q}_{c}=0.
$$

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-50t/9},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{50}{9}\alpha =\frac{3}{10}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{27}{500}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{27}{500}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-50t/9}+\frac{27}{500}.

- The constant ${q}_{p}=\frac{27}{500}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to \infty ,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
A series RC circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $24\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $75\,Ω,$ and a capacitance of $0.002\,\text{F}.$ Find, in coulombs rounded to three decimal places, the circuit capacitor's charge after $0.06$ seconds, given that the initial charge is $\frac{1}{40}$ coulombs.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=75\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=75I=75\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24=75\,\frac{dq}{dt}+500q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{20}{3}q=\frac{8}{25}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+\frac{20}{3}{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-20t/3},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha .
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${q}_{p}=\alpha $ and $\frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt}=(\alpha )^{′}=0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0+\frac{20}{3}\alpha =\frac{8}{25}\,⟹\,\alpha =\frac{6}{125}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{6}{125}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-20t/3}+\frac{6}{125}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{40}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $q(0)=\frac{1}{40},$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0) & =\frac{1}{40} \\ A{e}^{-20(0)/3}+\frac{6}{125} & =\frac{1}{40} \\ A & =-\frac{23}{1000}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $q(t):$

$$
q(t)=\frac{6}{125}-\frac{23}{1000}{e}^{-20t/3}
$$

Finally, the charge on the capacitor in the circuit after $t=0.06$ seconds, in coulombs, is

$$
q(0.06)=\frac{6}{125}-\frac{23}{1000}{e}^{-20(0.06)/3}≈0.033,
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/94befb5500eff8908ded191ea1bd018347718823c34f9fbf369791d37708c72c.png)

Consider the RC circuit shown above. Given that the charge $q(t)$ of the capacitor at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
q(t)=A{e}^{-t}+\frac{P}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{Q}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)
$$

where $A,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $200\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=200\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=200I=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +\beta =\frac{1}{25}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ \alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{425},\beta =\frac{1}{425}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-4,Q=1,$ and

$$
P+Q=-4+1=-3.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/b1933db5df10c1a3faf07f1d459a7736be682a3d01ab85e48214da21e7a9d1d5.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state charge for the RC circuit shown above, in coulombs, rounded to two decimal places. 

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $80\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $20\,Ω,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\frac{1}{100}\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{(\frac{1}{100})}=100q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
80\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}+100q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+5q=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+5{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(5\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +5\beta =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 5\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{16}{41},\beta =\frac{20}{41}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{16}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{20}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}-\frac{16}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{20}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{16}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{20}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{16}{41}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{20}{41}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{16}{41})}^{2}+{(\frac{20}{41})}^{2}}≈0.62,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/a4182416a97e5f0111b0823d6699f0ed39125f60289d7c7ebbb5f98d51d1a0f6.png)

Find, in coulombs, the amplitude of the steady-state charge for the RC circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $20\,Ω,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\frac{1}{60}\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{(\frac{1}{60})}=60q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}+60q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+3q=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+3{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+3(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +3\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 3\alpha +4\beta =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{3}{25},\beta =\frac{4}{25}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-3t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{4}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{25})}^{2}+{(\frac{4}{25})}^{2}}=0.2.
$$

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\sin(3t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $80\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.0025\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 80\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 80I = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.0025} = 400q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\sin(3t) = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 400q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin(3t).
$$

Find an equation for the charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) **only**, and given that the initial charge is $\dfrac{1}{50}\,\textrm{C}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 80\,\Omega.$So,

$$
V_R = 80I = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.00125} = 800q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24 = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 800q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q = \dfrac3{10}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-10t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $q_p = \alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + 10\alpha = \dfrac3{10}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac3{100}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $q_p(t) = \dfrac3{100}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-10t} + \dfrac3{100}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\dfrac{1}{50}\,\textrm{C}$ on the capacitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $q(0) = \dfrac{1}{50},$ and solve for $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0) & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A{e}^{-10(0)}+\frac{3}{100} & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A & =-\frac{1}{100}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(t) & =-\frac{1}{100}{e}^{-10t}+\frac{3}{100} \\  & =\frac{1}{100}(3-{e}^{-10t})\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c = -\dfrac1{100}e^{-10t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The constant $q_p = \dfrac3{100}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to\infty,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/962694e1706c47a4b060da6636e0b6e2f1653cb94137dca8dc59781cf74bd252.png)

Find the amplitude of the steady-state charge for the RC circuit shown above, in coulombs, rounded to two decimal places. 

*Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $90\cos(6t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $30\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor with capacitance $\dfrac1{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
So far, we've used differential equations to model quantities in circuits containing resistors and inductors. Now, we'll focus on circuits containing resistors and capacitors.

A **capacitor** is a component of an electrical circuit that opposes *changes* in voltage across it by storing energy in an electric field.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/3729fc4786e8677a1a7bf20aa013d6c6943c6d69c73adc63dd743c3918e65db4.png)

The capacitance $C$ (measured in farads) of a capacitor determines how much charge $q$ (measured in coulombs) the capacitor stores for a given voltage, $V_C,$ according to the equation 

$$
q = CV_C.
$$

An **RC circuit** is an electrical circuit that contains both a resistor and a capacitor, most commonly in series with a voltage source. An example, with current $I(t),$ is shown below, consisting of a resistance $R,$ in ohms, a capacitance $C,$ in farads, and a source electromotive force (emf) $E,$ in volts.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/feef8e5b715b6b0442dc27a65886d611b27d4d912842f992790e6309a78afda4.png)

Let $q(t)$ denote the charge on the capacitor, measured in coulombs, as a function of time $t.$ Can we find a differential equation that best describes the charge $q(t)$ on the capacitor?

First, note that since current is the rate at which electric charge flows, the circuit's current is the derivative of charge with respect to time: 

$$
I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Now, recall Kirchhoff's Voltage law, which states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops around the loop.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The resistor *opposes the flow of current*, hence producing a voltage drop $V_R$ proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R{:}$

$$
V_R = RI = R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

- The capacitor *opposes changes in voltage*, hence producing a voltage drop $V_C$ related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ So, 

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{C}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, the source voltage $E$ is the sum of the voltage drops: $E = V_R + V_C.$

As a result, the basic equation governing the amount of charge on the capacitor $q$ in the circuit is

$$
E = R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{q}{C}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{RC}q = \dfrac{E}{R}.
$$

Note that since $I(t) = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ solving for $q(t)$ also tells us the current in the circuit.

tutorials.name: A Worked Example
tutorials.problem:
Consider a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\sin(2t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistance of $40\,\Omega,$ and a capacitance of $0.0025\,\textrm{F}.$ Let's find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds).

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.
In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 40\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 40I = 40\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.0025} = 400q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\sin(2t) = 40\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 400q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q = \dfrac{1}{5}\sin(2t).
$$

tutorials.name: Steady-State Charges for Constant Voltage RC Circuits
tutorials.problem:
In a first-order linear differential equation, the solution naturally splits into a transient term that decays over time and a steady-state term that remains as $t \to \infty$.

In an RC circuit with a constant electromotive force (EMF), this steady-state value corresponds to the charge the capacitor approaches as $t \to \infty,$ regardless of the initial charge. Physically, this represents the maximum charge the capacitor can store under a constant applied voltage.

To demonstrate how to identify the steady-state charge directly from the general solution of an RC circuit model, suppose the charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, in a series RC circuit is governed by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 12q = \dfrac{7}{10}.
$$

This equation is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} +12q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-12t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $q_p = \alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + 12\alpha = \dfrac{7}{10}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac{7}{120}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $q_p(t) = \dfrac{7}{120}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-12t} + \dfrac{7}{120}.
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c = Ae^{-12t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The constant $q_p = \dfrac{7}{120}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to\infty,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

Therefore, the steady-state charge (the charge the capacitor approaches as time increases) is ${\dfrac{7}{120}}$ coulombs.

tutorials.name: Steady-State Charges for Sinusoidal Voltage RC Circuits
tutorials.problem:
In a first-order linear RC circuit driven by a sinusoidal voltage, the solution consists of a transient charge, which decays over time, and a steady-state charge, which oscillates with the same frequency as the input.

As time increases, the transient charge vanishes, leaving a steady-state charge that oscillates periodically and is independent of the initial condition.

To demonstrate, let's find the amplitude of the steady-state charge in the RC circuit below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/fc700238d93fd6529c7113cd1a650e8c03d796e606afd4b655123cd04ed11cc7.png)

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\cos(4t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $50\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $\dfrac{1}{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 50\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 50I = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac{1}{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\cos(4t) = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q = \dfrac{2}{5}\cos(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(4t) + \beta\sin(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+3(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +3\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 3\alpha +4\beta =\frac{2}{5}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{6}{125}$ and $\beta = \dfrac{8}{125}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-3t} + \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t) \approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{6}{125}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{8}{125}\right)^2} =0.08\,\textrm{coulombs}.
$$

This amplitude represents the maximum magnitude of the oscillating steady-state charge on the capacitor.

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
So far, we've used differential equations to model quantities in circuits containing resistors and inductors. Now, we'll focus on circuits containing resistors and capacitors.

A **capacitor** is a component of an electrical circuit that opposes *changes* in voltage across it by storing energy in an electric field.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/3729fc4786e8677a1a7bf20aa013d6c6943c6d69c73adc63dd743c3918e65db4.png)

The capacitance $C$ (measured in farads) of a capacitor determines how much charge $q$ (measured in coulombs) the capacitor stores for a given voltage, $V_C,$ according to the equation 

$$
q = CV_C.
$$

An **RC circuit** is an electrical circuit that contains both a resistor and a capacitor, most commonly in series with a voltage source. An example, with current $I(t),$ is shown below, consisting of a resistance $R,$ in ohms, a capacitance $C,$ in farads, and a source electromotive force (emf) $E,$ in volts.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/feef8e5b715b6b0442dc27a65886d611b27d4d912842f992790e6309a78afda4.png)

Let $q(t)$ denote the charge on the capacitor, measured in coulombs, as a function of time $t.$ Can we find a differential equation that best describes the charge $q(t)$ on the capacitor?

First, note that since current is the rate at which electric charge flows, the circuit's current is the derivative of charge with respect to time: 

$$
I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Now, recall Kirchhoff's Voltage law, which states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops around the loop.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The resistor *opposes the flow of current*, hence producing a voltage drop $V_R$ proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R{:}$

$$
V_R = RI = R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

- The capacitor *opposes changes in voltage*, hence producing a voltage drop $V_C$ related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ So, 

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{C}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, the source voltage $E$ is the sum of the voltage drops: $E = V_R + V_C.$

As a result, the basic equation governing the amount of charge on the capacitor $q$ in the circuit is

$$
E = R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{q}{C}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{RC}q = \dfrac{E}{R}.
$$

Note that since $I(t) = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t},$ solving for $q(t)$ also tells us the current in the circuit.

tutorial.name: A Worked Example
tutorial.problem:
Consider a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\sin(2t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistance of $40\,\Omega,$ and a capacitance of $0.0025\,\textrm{F}.$ Let's find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds).

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.
In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 40\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 40I = 40\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.0025} = 400q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\sin(2t) = 40\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 400q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q = \dfrac{1}{5}\sin(2t).
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge q (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
dqdt+200q=15
b
dqdt+15q=2
c
dqdt+2q=30
d
dqdt+1200q=30
e
dqdt+2q=15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 20V, a resistor of resistance 100Ω, and a capacitor of capacitance 0.005F.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=100Ω. So, VR=100I=100dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.005=200q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 20=100dqdt+200q, which gives dqdt+2q=15.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $24\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $100\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.001\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=100\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=100I=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.001}=1000q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)=100\,\frac{dq}{dt}+1000q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+10q=\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge q (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
dqdt+10q=24sin⁡(t)
b
dqdt+1000q=625sin⁡(t)
c
dqdt+10q=625sin⁡(t)
d
dqdt+110q=625sin⁡(t)
e
dqdt+1000q=24sin⁡(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 24sin⁡(t)V, a resistor of resistance 100Ω, and a capacitor of capacitance 0.001F.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=100Ω. So, VR=100I=100dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.001=1000q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 24sin⁡(t)=100dqdt+1000q, which gives dqdt+10q=625sin⁡(t).

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $60\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.003\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=60\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=60I=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.003}=\frac{1000}{3}q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
18\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=60\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{1000}{3}q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{50}{9}q=\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Question 3
?

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge q (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
dqdt+509q=310cos⁡(2t)
b
dqdt+10003q=18cos⁡(2t)
c
dqdt+509q=18cos⁡(2t)
d
dqdt+10003q=310cos⁡(2t)
e
dqdt+950q=310cos⁡(2t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 18cos⁡(2t)V, a resistor of resistance 60Ω, and a capacitor of capacitance 0.003F.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=60Ω. So, VR=60I=60dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.003=10003q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 18cos⁡(2t)=60dqdt+10003q, which gives dqdt+509q=310cos⁡(2t).

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $25\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=25\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=25I=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
6\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)=25\,\frac{dq}{dt}+250q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+10q=\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge q (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
dqdt+110q=625cos⁡(5t)
b
dqdt+250q=625cos⁡(5t)
c
dqdt+250q=6cos⁡(5t)
d
dqdt+10q=6cos⁡(5t)
e
dqdt+10q=625cos⁡(5t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 6cos⁡(5t)V, a resistor of resistance 25Ω, and a capacitor of capacitance 0.004F.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=25Ω. So, VR=25I=25dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.004=250q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 6cos⁡(5t)=25dqdt+250q, which gives dqdt+10q=625cos⁡(5t).

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RC Circuit
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $15\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $250\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.004\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=250\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=250I=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.004}=250q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
15=250\,\frac{dq}{dt}+250q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{3}{50}.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge q (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
dqdt+q=30
b
dqdt+250q=350
c
dqdt+q=350
d
dqdt+350q=1
e
dqdt+1250q=30
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 15V, a resistor of resistance 250Ω, and a capacitor of capacitance 0.004F.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=250Ω. So, VR=250I=250dqdt.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=q0.004=250q.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge q on the capacitor is 15=250dqdt+250q, which gives dqdt+q=350.

tutorial.name: Steady-State Charges for Constant Voltage RC Circuits
tutorial.problem:
In a first-order linear differential equation, the solution naturally splits into a transient term that decays over time and a steady-state term that remains as $t \to \infty$.

In an RC circuit with a constant electromotive force (EMF), this steady-state value corresponds to the charge the capacitor approaches as $t \to \infty,$ regardless of the initial charge. Physically, this represents the maximum charge the capacitor can store under a constant applied voltage.

To demonstrate how to identify the steady-state charge directly from the general solution of an RC circuit model, suppose the charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, in a series RC circuit is governed by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 12q = \dfrac{7}{10}.
$$

This equation is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} +12q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-12t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $q_p = \alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + 12\alpha = \dfrac{7}{10}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac{7}{120}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $q_p(t) = \dfrac{7}{120}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-12t} + \dfrac{7}{120}.
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c = Ae^{-12t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The constant $q_p = \dfrac{7}{120}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to\infty,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

Therefore, the steady-state charge (the charge the capacitor approaches as time increases) is ${\dfrac{7}{120}}$ coulombs.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 80\,\Omega.$So,

$$
V_R = 80I = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{0.00125} = 800q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
24 = 80\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 800q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q = \dfrac3{10}.
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 10q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-10t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha.
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $q_p = \alpha$ and $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} = (\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:

$$
0 + 10\alpha = \dfrac3{10}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \alpha = \dfrac3{100}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is $q_p(t) = \dfrac3{100}.$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-10t} + \dfrac3{100}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\dfrac{1}{50}\,\textrm{C}$ on the capacitor. So, we can apply the initial condition $q(0) = \dfrac{1}{50},$ and solve for $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0) & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A{e}^{-10(0)}+\frac{3}{100} & =\frac{1}{50} \\ A & =-\frac{1}{100}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $q(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}q(t) & =-\frac{1}{100}{e}^{-10t}+\frac{3}{100} \\  & =\frac{1}{100}(3-{e}^{-10t})\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c = -\dfrac1{100}e^{-10t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The constant $q_p = \dfrac3{100}$ is the *steady-state charge*. As $t\to\infty,$ the charge $q$ approaches the value of the steady-state charge.

$$

$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-6t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$

$$

tutorial.name: Steady-State Charges for Sinusoidal Voltage RC Circuits
tutorial.problem:
In a first-order linear RC circuit driven by a sinusoidal voltage, the solution consists of a transient charge, which decays over time, and a steady-state charge, which oscillates with the same frequency as the input.

As time increases, the transient charge vanishes, leaving a steady-state charge that oscillates periodically and is independent of the initial condition.

To demonstrate, let's find the amplitude of the steady-state charge in the RC circuit below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184069/assets/fc700238d93fd6529c7113cd1a650e8c03d796e606afd4b655123cd04ed11cc7.png)

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\cos(4t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor with resistance $50\,\Omega,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $\dfrac{1}{150}\,\textrm{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 50\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 50I = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac{1}{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
20\cos(4t) = 50\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q = \dfrac{2}{5}\cos(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 3q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(4t) + \beta\sin(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+3(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +3\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ 3\alpha +4\beta =\frac{2}{5}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{6}{125}$ and $\beta = \dfrac{8}{125}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-3t} + \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-3t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t) \approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{6}{125}\cos(4t) + \dfrac{8}{125}\sin(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{6}{125}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{8}{125}\right)^2} =0.08\,\textrm{coulombs}.
$$

This amplitude represents the maximum magnitude of the oscillating steady-state charge on the capacitor.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I = \dfrac{\textrm d q}{\textrm d t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R = 30\,\Omega.$ So,

$$
V_R = 30I = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore,

$$
V_C = \dfrac{q}{\left(\dfrac1{150}\right)} = 150q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
90\cos(6t) = 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 150q,
$$

which gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q = 3\cos(6t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 5q_c = 0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $6t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $6t,$ i.e.,

$$
q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(6t) + \beta\sin(6t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))+5(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ (-6\alpha +5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)+(5\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6\alpha +5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)) \\ 5\alpha +6\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha = \dfrac{15}{61}, \beta = \dfrac{18}{61}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-5t} + \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity $q_c(t) = Ae^{-5t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t \to \infty.$

- The function $q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to\infty,$ we have

$$
q(t)\approx q_p(t) = \dfrac{15}{61}\cos(6t) + \dfrac{18}{61}\sin(6t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{15}{61}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{18}{61}\right)^2} \approx 0.38,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

The diagram shows a series RC circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor with resistance $200\,Ω,$ and a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. 

$$
I=\frac{\text{d}q}{\text{d}t}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RC circuit, there are two voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=200\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=200I=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+200q,
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dq}{dt}+q=\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

This is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. So, to find the general solution, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ is a constant of integration.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))+(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-4\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+(\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\alpha +\beta =\frac{1}{25}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\ \alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{4}{425},\beta =\frac{1}{425}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}-\frac{4}{425}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{1}{425}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-4,Q=1,$ and

$$
P+Q=-4+1=-3.
$$
