Question 19
?

A group of students' math test results are normally distributed with a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 6. Furthermore, their science test results are normally distributed with a mean of 65 and a standard deviation of 10, while their language test results are normally distributed with a mean of 55 and a standard deviation of 15. Find the probability that a randomly selected student's combined score is more than 200. You may assume that the scores on each test are independent.

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z0.000.010.020.030.04
0.5 0.6915 0.6950 0.6985 0.7019 0.7054
0.6 0.7257 0.7291 0.7324 0.7357 0.7389
0.7 0.7580 0.7611 0.7642 0.7673 0.7704
0.8 0.7881 0.7910 0.7939 0.7967 0.7995
a
0.3119
b
0.2676
c
0.2389
d
0.2981
e
0.3446
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let X1, X2, and X3 denote the student's math, science, and language test results, respectively. Then, we have

X1∼N(70,62),X2∼N(65,102),X3∼N(55,152).

Let the random variable Y denote the total score of a randomly selected student. So, we have

Y=X1+X2+X3.

The random variable Y is normally distributed, where

E[Y]=(70+65+55)=190,Var[Y]=62+102+152=36+100+225=361.

Therefore, Y∼N(190,361).

In order to find P(Y>200), we convert Y to a standard normal random variable by z-scoring: P(Y>200)=P(Z>200−190361)≈P(Z>0.53)=1−P(Z<0.53)=1−Φ(0.53)

Using the z-table, we see that

Φ(0.53)≈0.7019.

Therefore,

P(Y>200)≈1−Φ(0.53)≈1−0.7019=0.2981.

solution.reasoning: The combined score is normal with mean 70+65+55=190 and variance 6²+10²+15²=361, so its standard deviation is 19. Thus P(Y>200)=1−Φ(10/19). question.name: Question 20
question.problem:
A course grade is calculated by adding the results of a written test, oral test, and colloquium, contributing $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%,$ respectively to the final grade. 

The written test results are normally distributed with a mean of $64$ and a standard deviation of $8.$ The oral test results are normally distributed with a mean of $50$ and a standard deviation of $10$, while the results of the colloquium are normally distributed with a mean of $60$ and a standard deviation of $10.$ Find the probability that a randomly selected student achieves a grade greater than $70.$ You may assume that the scores on each test are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9713\,$ | $\,0.9719\,$ | $\,0.9726\,$ | $\,0.9732\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ | $\,0.9788\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9821\,$ | $\,0.9826\,$ | $\,0.9830\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the written test, oral test, and colloquium results, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(64,{8}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(50,{10}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(60,{10}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the final grade of a randomly selected student. Since the written, oral, and colloquium contribute $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%$, respectively, to the final grade, we have

$$
Y=0.5{X}_{1}+0.3{X}_{2}+0.2{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =0.5\cdot 64+0.3\cdot 50+0.2\cdot 60 \\  & =59, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =(0.5)^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}+(0.3)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2}+(0.2)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2} \\  & =0.25\cdot 64+0.09\cdot 10+0.04\cdot 100 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ∼N(59,29).\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $P(Y>70),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & =P(Z>\frac{70-59}{\sqrt{29}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>2.04) \\  & =1-P(Z<2.04) \\  & =1-Φ(2.04)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.04)≈0.9793.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & ≈1-Φ(2.04) \\  & ≈1-0.9793 \\  & =0.0207.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the written test, oral test, and colloquium results, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(64,{8}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(50,{10}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(60,{10}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the final grade of a randomly selected student. Since the written, oral, and colloquium contribute $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%$, respectively, to the final grade, we have

$$
Y=0.5{X}_{1}+0.3{X}_{2}+0.2{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =0.5\cdot 64+0.3\cdot 50+0.2\cdot 60 \\  & =59, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =(0.5)^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}+(0.3)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2}+(0.2)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2} \\  & =0.25\cdot 64+0.09\cdot 10+0.04\cdot 100 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ∼N(59,29).\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $P(Y>70),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & =P(Z>\frac{70-59}{\sqrt{29}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>2.04) \\  & =1-P(Z<2.04) \\  & =1-Φ(2.04)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.04)≈0.9793.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & ≈1-Φ(2.04) \\  & ≈1-0.9793 \\  & =0.0207.\end{aligned}
$$

z 0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04
1.9 0.9713 0.9719 0.9726 0.9732 0.9738
2.0 0.9772 0.9778 0.9783 0.9788 0.9793

EXPLANATION

X1∼N(64,82),X2∼N(50,102),X3∼N(60,102).

Y=0.5X1+0.3X2+0.2X3.

The random variable Y is normally distributed, where

E[Y]=0.5⋅64+0.3⋅50+0.2⋅60=59,Var[Y]=(0.5)2⋅82+(0.3)2⋅102+(0.2)2⋅102=0.25⋅64+0.09⋅10+0.04⋅100=29.

Therefore, Y∼N(59,29).

In order to find P(Y>70), we convert Y to a standard normal random variable by z-scoring: P(Y>70)=P(Z>70−5929)≈P(Z>2.04)=1−P(Z<2.04)=1−Φ(2.04)

Using the z-table, we see that

Φ(2.04)≈0.9793.

Therefore,

P(Y>70)≈1−Φ(2.04)≈1−0.9793=0.0207.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/320a45751b2e718c66bb721cfcd78a2d206f08a9998fbbffddb1581ee995cf34.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}x\,dy-y\,dx,$ where $D$ is the region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}x\,dy-y\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-(-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot ({4}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (16-4) \\  & =2\cdot 12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/e9892ef4efa3481ad02f7b8e38f1bae1876b196627204521d011656010297281.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=6,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=4,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/b20b2b911c2a417c26fa951d9b28efa296c265df25e9d06b635ef4846267b93b.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+6+4 \\  & =26.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/393bed476f2e8d84fc7e5dc721d77749f7f259834e03a94a48a08533ae9befa6.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy,$ where $D$ is the region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2y$ and $Q(x,y)=4x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (6\cdot 4-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (24-4) \\  & =2\cdot 20 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/0db447407835f74476edd20ed5327ff3cc570905f744bbc6c29a66926913ecb5.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}(1-4y)\,dx+(2+5x)\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=1-4y$ and $Q(x,y)=2+5x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-(-4))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =9\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =9\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =45\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}x\,dy-y\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-(-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot ({4}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (16-4) \\  & =2\cdot 12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=1-4y$ and $Q(x,y)=2+5x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-(-4))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =9\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =9\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =45\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/e9892ef4efa3481ad02f7b8e38f1bae1876b196627204521d011656010297281.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=16,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=6,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=4,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/b20b2b911c2a417c26fa951d9b28efa296c265df25e9d06b635ef4846267b93b.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =16+6+4 \\  & =26.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that F is a vector field on R2 defined over the region D above. Given that

∮C1F⋅dr=16,∮C2F⋅dr=6,∮C3F⋅dr=4,

where C1 is oriented counterclockwise and C2 and C3 are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ∮∂DF⋅dr.

a
14
b
6
c
18
d
26
e
13
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each positively oriented boundary.

Remember that:

  • the positive direction is counterclockwise for the outer curve C1 (because the region D is always on the left as we traverse C1 counterclockwise), and

  • the positive direction is clockwise for the inner curves C2 and C3 (because the region D is always on the left as we traverse C2 and C3 clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

Therefore, we have

∮∂DF⋅dr=∮C1F⋅dr+∮C2F⋅dr+∮C3F⋅dr=16+6+4=26.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/393bed476f2e8d84fc7e5dc721d77749f7f259834e03a94a48a08533ae9befa6.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy,$ where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2y$ and $Q(x,y)=4x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}2y\,dx+4x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (6\cdot 4-{2}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (24-4) \\  & =2\cdot 20 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing D, then Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that P(x,y)=2y and Q(x,y)=4x. So,

∂P∂y=2,∂Q∂x=4.

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

∮∂D2ydx+4xdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(4−2)dA=∬D2dA=2∬DdA=2⋅Area(D)=2⋅(6⋅4−22)=2⋅(24−4)=2⋅20=40.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/49b14da54c952d0585f7aa894d618838ddc91beb65216e0c18c014ba5ad268d7.png)

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=9,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-4,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-6,
$$

where ${C}_{1}$ is oriented counterclockwise and ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of ${∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.$
question.worked_solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/a8e93055fb9a460ab7757475c9c381c191204eae72231921da870b8d727bf988.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =9+(-4)+(-6) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14184009/assets/0db447407835f74476edd20ed5327ff3cc570905f744bbc6c29a66926913ecb5.png)

Calculate ${∮}_{∂D}(1-4y)\,dx+(2+5x)\,dy,$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=1-4y$ and $Q(x,y)=2+5x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-(-4))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9\,\text{d}A \\  & =9\,\text{Area}(D) \\  & =9\cdot (\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & =9\cdot 5\pi  \\  & =45\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate ∮∂D(1−4y)dx+(2+5x)dy, where D is the annular region shown above.

a
45π
b
52π
c
54π
d
48π
e
60π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing D, then Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that P(x,y)=1−4y and Q(x,y)=2+5x. So,

∂P∂y=−4,∂Q∂x=5.

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

∮∂Ddx+xdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(5−(−4))dA=∬D9dA=9Area(D)=9⋅(π⋅32−π⋅22)=9⋅5π=45π.

Which of the graphs above represent proportional relationships?
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the graph of a proportional relationship is always a straight line that passes through the origin $(0,0).$

Of the given graphs, none of the graphs fits this description.

- Graphs I, II, and III  are not straight lines.

- Graph  IV does not pass through the origin $(0,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/1778ff7ea1ee5b1bcf918992d8b2be700362031cd7d142b00b3dc79470983eb0.png)

The graph above shows a proportional relationship between the time $x$ (in minutes) that water flows through a hose into a tank and the corresponding amount $y$ of water (in gallons) that has entered the tank during that period. What is the unit rate of the water flow?
questions.worked_solution:
The unit rate in gallons per minute is simply the constant of proportionality for the given proportional relationship.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(4,15).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/d063a3c2ebf77d1132349b7e48f883632d97720d491a4a5c9158b49c5809258e.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{15}{4}
$$

Therefore, the water flow unit rate is $\frac{15}{4}$ gallons per minute.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/d3de064ab8dbab633656b19cfc340f6ce43f4df8a7e18834019e6301ef67ab00.png)

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $h$ and $x.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?
questions.worked_solution:
Since $h$ varies directly with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
h=kx.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $h=6$ and $x=3.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =k\cdot 3 \\ \frac{6}{3} & =k \\ 2 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
h=2x.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/472c0aebabed979b97d9d68648785773f0715da9e8cf88c1f1ee912a27d6cb77.png)

The graph above shows that the distance $d$ an electric train travels is directly proportional to the number of hours $t$ since its journey started. Find a direct variation equation that describes the relationship between $d$ and $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $d$ varies directly with $t,$ we use the equation

$$
d=kt.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $t=4$ and $d=840.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}840 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{840}{4} & =k \\ 210 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
d=210t.
$$

Example: 
                    Computing a Constant of Proportionality or Unit Rate
canonical_examples.problem:
The graph below shows a proportional relationship. What is the constant of proportionality?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/6298e9ee004e642d05d065d1fc2fd325f07d313ac736ef15b190c1b9c90d1019.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(4,3).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/d573d9aad231622b2e5dc42a8672d973e5fda518d75894f3bafb0b1a97532d24.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k = \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{3}{4}
$$

Therefore, the constant of proportionality is $k=\dfrac{3}{4}.$

The graph above shows the relationship between the displacement $d,$ in centimeters, of a particular spring when a mass $m,$ in kilograms, is attached to it. Find a direct variation equation that describes the relationship between $d$ and $m.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $d$ varies directly with $m,$ we use the equation

$$
d = km.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $m=5$ and $d=20.$ So, we substitute this data into the above equation to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & =k\cdot 5 \\ \frac{20}{5} & =k \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
d=4m.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
How does a proportional relationship look when we plot it in the $(x,y)$ plane?

To answer this, let's consider the following proportional relationship:

$$
y = 2x
$$

To plot a graph, we first need a table of values. 

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ |  |
| $1$ |  |
| $2$ |  |
| $3$ |  |

Filling in the $y$-values using the equation $y = 2x,$ we get the following:

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ |
| $1$ | $2$ |
| $2$ | $4$ |
| $3$ | $6$ |

So, we have the following $(x,y)$ coordinates:

$$
(0,0), \quad (1,2),  \quad (2,4),  \quad (3,6)
$$

If we plot these points in the coordinate plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/a8cd951c66c67b8f28b791011c7553675b3112029d9ebe4b19769127b5e75bd5.png)

This leads us to the following important fact:

*The graph of any proportional relationship is a straight line that passes through the origin $(0,0)$.*

tutorials.name: Alternative Notations and Terminology
tutorials.problem:
When there is a proportional relationship between $x$ and $y,$ we can express this using the **proportionality symbol** $\propto,$ as follows:

$$
y \propto x
$$

Note that the following statements are all equivalent:

- $y = kx$

- $y$ **varies directly** with $x$

- $y$ is **directly proportional** to $x$

- $y \propto x$

tutorial.problem:
When there is a proportional relationship between $x$ and $y,$ we can express this using the **proportionality symbol** $\propto,$ as follows:

$$
y \propto x
$$

Note that the following statements are all equivalent:

- $y = kx$

- $y$ **varies directly** with $x$

- $y$ is **directly proportional** to $x$

- $y \propto x$

Since $d$ varies directly with $m,$ we use the equation

$$
d = km.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $m=5$ and $d=20.$ So, we substitute this data into the above equation to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & =k\cdot 5 \\ \frac{20}{5} & =k \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables h and x. Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?

a
h=−2x
b
h=2x
c
h=−12x
d
h=3x
e
h=12x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since h varies directly with x, we use the equation

h=kx.

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with h=6 and x=3. So, we substitute this data into the equation to find k:

6=k⋅363=k2=k

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by h=2x.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since $d$ varies directly with $t,$ we use the equation

$$
d=kt.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $t=4$ and $d=840.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}840 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{840}{4} & =k \\ 210 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
d=210t.
$$

Graphs I and III are curved, and graph IV has a positive y-intercept. The supplied worked solution is for a different example and does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

Which of the graphs above represent proportional relationships?
feedback.worked_solution:
Remember that the graph of a proportional relationship is always a straight line that passes through the origin $(0,0).$

Of the given graphs, only graph II fits this description.

- Graphs I and III are not straight lines.

- Graph IV does not pass through the origin $(0,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/1778ff7ea1ee5b1bcf918992d8b2be700362031cd7d142b00b3dc79470983eb0.png)

The graph above shows a proportional relationship between the time $x$ (in minutes) that water flows through a hose into a tank and the corresponding amount $y$ of water (in gallons) that has entered the tank during that period. What is the unit rate of the water flow?
question.worked_solution:
The unit rate in gallons per minute is simply the constant of proportionality for the given proportional relationship.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(4,15).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/d063a3c2ebf77d1132349b7e48f883632d97720d491a4a5c9158b49c5809258e.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{15}{4}
$$

Therefore, the water flow unit rate is $\frac{15}{4}$ gallons per minute.

feedback.html:
Question 3
?

The graph above shows a proportional relationship between the time x (in minutes) that water flows through a hose into a tank and the corresponding amount y of water (in gallons) that has entered the tank during that period. What is the unit rate of the water flow?

a
4 gallons per minute
b
154 gallons per minute
c
163 gallons per minute
d
52 gallons per minute
e
94 gallons per minute
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The unit rate in gallons per minute is simply the constant of proportionality for the given proportional relationship.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point (x,y) on the graph. Here, let's choose the point (4,15).

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the y-coordinate to the x-coordinate, as follows:

k=yx=154

Therefore, the water flow unit rate is 154 gallons per minute.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/df0b1950f3093cf368cdd463b1c137df98bae4eb29d7d51f2ce7b34a17c93c77.png)

The graph above shows a proportional relationship. What is the constant of proportionality?
question.worked_solution:
To find the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(5,4).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/468695422e5c641a076c8f2889f926a7c633c69e98c96fdefb07b2c19c2acbdc.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{4}{5}
$$

Therefore, the constant of proportionality is $k=\frac{4}{5}.$

question.worked_solution:
Since $h$ varies directly with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
h=kx.
$$

$$

$$
h=2x.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables h and x. Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?

a
h=−2x
b
h=2x
c
h=−12x
d
h=3x
e
h=12x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since h varies directly with x, we use the equation

h=kx.

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with h=6 and x=3. So, we substitute this data into the equation to find k:

6=k⋅363=k2=k

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by h=2x.
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Direct Variation Equation from a Graph

solution.reasoning: Direct variation has the form h=kx. The marked point is (x,h)=(3,6), so k=6/3=2 and h=2x, choice b. The supplied worked solution concerns a different example; Math Academy's answer for this question is not captured.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14184158/assets/d3de064ab8dbab633656b19cfc340f6ce43f4df8a7e18834019e6301ef67ab00.png)

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $h$ and $x.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $h$ varies directly with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
h=kx.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $h=6$ and $x=3.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =k\cdot 3 \\ \frac{6}{3} & =k \\ 2 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
h=2x.
$$

The graph above shows that the distance d an electric train travels is directly proportional to the number of hours t since its journey started. Find a direct variation equation that describes the relationship between d and t.

a
d=100t
b
d=800t+40
c
d=240t
d
d=210t
e
d=840t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since d varies directly with t, we use the equation

d=kt.

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with t=4 and d=840. So, we substitute this data into the equation to find k:

840=k⋅48404=k210=k

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by d=210t.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $d$ varies directly with $t,$ we use the equation

$$
d=kt.
$$

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with $t=4$ and $d=840.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}840 & =k\cdot 4 \\ \frac{840}{4} & =k \\ 210 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
d=210t.
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The graph above shows that the distance d an electric train travels is directly proportional to the number of hours t since its journey started. Find a direct variation equation that describes the relationship between d and t.

a
d=100t
b
d=800t+40
c
d=240t
d
d=210t
e
d=840t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since d varies directly with t, we use the equation

d=kt.

Next, we notice that there is a point on the graph with t=4 and d=840. So, we substitute this data into the equation to find k:

840=k⋅48404=k210=k

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by d=210t.
question.knowledge_point: Finding a Direct Variation Equation from a Graph

solution.reasoning: Direct variation has the form d=kt. The marked point gives t=4 and d=840, so k=840/4=210 km/h. Thus d=210t, choice d. The supplied worked solution concerns a different example; Math Academy's answer for this question is not captured.

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =1, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(-1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 4xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2{x}^{2}+2yz \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 2yz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+1 & ={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+z+C.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the rectangle $R$ can be represented as a union of two smaller rectangles, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =((-1,1)\cup (1,3))\times (0,2) \\  & =((-1,1)\times (0,2))\cup ((1,3)\times (0,2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{(-1,1)\times (0,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{(1,3)\times (0,2)}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{(-1,1)\times (0,2)}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A\text{ }+{∬}_{(1,3)\times (0,2)}{2}^{xy}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{4}.$

For the side ${S}_{4},$ we have $u=0$ and $1\ge v\ge 0.$ Substituting $u=0$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(2v(1-u-v),\,\frac{1-v}{1+u}) \\  & =(2v(1-0-v),\,\frac{1-v}{1+0}) \\  & =(2v(1-v),\,1-v).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{4}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=2v(1-v),\,y=1-v,\,1\ge v\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x=2t(1-t),\,y=1-t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

These are parametric equations of a parabolic arc. Notice that if we eliminate $t$ from the equations, we get

$$
x=2(1-y)(y)\,⇒\,x=-2{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

which is a left-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

Moreover, the endpoints of ${S}_{4}$ are mapped to the $xy$-plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T:(0,1)\to (2(1)(1-0-1),\frac{1-1}{1+0})=(0,0) \\  & T:(0,0)\to (2(0)(1-0-0),\frac{1-0}{1+0})=(0,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of ${S}_{4}$ is an arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,0)$ to $(0,1).$

questions.worked_solution:
Remember, the order of the vectors in a basis is important.

Notice that 

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={{(\,2\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{1}}+{{(\,3\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{2}}+{{(\,6\,)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{b}_{3}}
$$

which means that

$$
x=2\cdot {b}_{1}+3\cdot {b}_{2}+6\cdot {b}_{3}
$$

and therefore 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{aligned}],
$$

Finally, ${x}_{2}=3.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=4{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $4,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $4$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =4\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-4det(A) \\  & =-4\cdot 6 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

6.Calculating a Determinant After Applying Several Elementary Operations?

Suppose A is a 5×5 matrix and det(A)=6. The matrix B is obtained from A by applying the elementary row operations R2↔R3 and R3:=4R3. What is the value of det(B)?

Question 3

Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={x2y2,if−1<x<1,0<y<2,2xy,if1<x<3,0<y<2. Then, ∬(−1,3)×(0,2)f(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2xydA
b
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)x2y2dA +∬(−1,1)×(0,2)2x+ydA
c
 ∬(−1,1)×(1,3)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2xydA
d
 ∬(−1,1)×(1,3)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2x+ydA
e
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)2xydA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)x2y2dA

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=2v(1-u-v),\,y=\frac{1-v}{1+u}.
$$

Which of the following is the image of the side ${S}_{4}$ under the action of $T?$

choices.value: An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,0)$ to $(0,1).$

Question 4

Consider the square region Δ in the uv-plane, given by Δ={(u,v):0≤u≤1,0≤v≤1},

and the transformation T, given by T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)), where x=2v(1−u−v),y=1−v1+u.

Which of the following is the image of the side S4 under the action of T?

a
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (0,0) to (0,1).
b
 An arc of a downward-opening parabola, traversed from (0,1) to (0,0).
c
 An arc of a downward-opening parabola, traversed from (1,0) to (0,1).
d
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (1,0) to (1,1).
e
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (0,1) to (0,0).

judgments.reasoning: Holding t constant gives ∂f/∂s=1(−cos t)+(−1)(sin t)=−(cos t+sin t). This matches my earlier answer, submitted option e, the revealed Correct grade, and Math Academy’s worked solution.

For f=2x²y+y²z+z+C, the partial derivatives are f_x=4xy, f_y=2x²+2yz, and f_z=y²+1, exactly the components of F. My earlier answer and submitted option e agree with both the revealed Correct grade and Math Academy’s worked solution.

Additivity splits the integral at x=1, using x²y² on the left and 2^{xy} on the right. My earlier answer and submitted option a match the Correct grade and worked solution. The solution’s literal set equality omits the line x=1; this area-zero omission does not change the integral, and any finite definition of f there gives the same result.

On S₄, u=0 and v decreases from 1 to 0. Thus y=1−v increases from 0 to 1 and x=2y(1−y)=1/2−2(y−1/2)², a left-opening parabola traversed from (0,0) to (0,1). My earlier answer and submitted option a agree with the Correct grade, worked solution, and image.

Swapping two rows reverses the determinant’s sign, and scaling one row by 4 multiplies it by 4. Thus det(B)=4(−6)=−24. My earlier answer and submitted option e agree with the Correct grade and Math Academy’s worked solution.

question.html:
Question 1

Let f(x,y)=x−y, where x=−scos⁡t and y=ssin⁡t. Calculate ∂f∂s.

a
 s(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)
b
 2cos⁡t
c
 cos⁡t−sin⁡t
d
 s(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)
e
 −(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)

solution.reasoning: Substituting gives f(s,t)=-s\cos t-s\sin t. Holding t constant, ∂f/∂s=-(\cos t+\sin t), which matches option e. The mathematical answer is certain, but no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

question.problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where $F(x,y,z)=4xy\,i+(2{x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+1)\,k.$

Question 2

Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), where F(x,y,z)=4xyi+(2x2+2yz)j+(y2+1)k.

a
 f(x,y,z)=4x2y+yz+z+C
b
 f(x,y,z)=xy2+yz2+x+C
c
 f(x,y,z)=x2y2+yz+xz+C
d
 f(x,y,z)=2x2z+y2z+y+C
e
 f(x,y,z)=2x2y+y2z+z+C

solution.reasoning: Integrating f_x=4xy gives f=2x²y+g(y,z). Then f_y=2x²+g_y=2x²+2yz implies g=y²z+h(z). Finally, f_z=y²+h′(z)=y²+1 gives h=z+C. Thus option e has the required gradient. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

question.html:
Question 3

Let the function f(x,y) be defined as f(x,y)={x2y2,if−1<x<1,0<y<2,2xy,if1<x<3,0<y<2. Then, ∬(−1,3)×(0,2)f(x,y) dA=

a
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2xydA
b
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)x2y2dA +∬(−1,1)×(0,2)2x+ydA
c
 ∬(−1,1)×(1,3)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2xydA
d
 ∬(−1,1)×(1,3)x2y2dA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)2x+ydA
e
 ∬(−1,1)×(0,2)2xydA +∬(1,3)×(0,2)x2y2dA

solution.reasoning: By additivity, split the region at x=1 and integrate each formula over its defining subregion. This gives option a. The unspecified values on x=1 do not affect the integral because that line has area zero. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

question.html:
Question 4

Consider the square region Δ in the uv-plane, given by Δ={(u,v):0≤u≤1,0≤v≤1},

and the transformation T, given by T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)), where x=2v(1−u−v),y=1−v1+u.

Which of the following is the image of the side S4 under the action of T?

a
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (0,0) to (0,1).
b
 An arc of a downward-opening parabola, traversed from (0,1) to (0,0).
c
 An arc of a downward-opening parabola, traversed from (1,0) to (0,1).
d
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (1,0) to (1,1).
e
 An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from (0,1) to (0,0).

solution.reasoning: The diagram orients S₄ downward: u=0 and v decreases from 1 to 0. Its image satisfies y=1-v and x=2v(1-v)=2y(1-y)=1/2-2(y-1/2)², a left-opening parabola. The endpoints map from (0,0) to (0,1), so option a is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

answers.correct_value: An arc of a left-opening parabola, traversed from $(0,0)$ to $(0,1).$

question.html:
Question 6

Suppose A is a 5×5 matrix and det(A)=6. The matrix B is obtained from A by applying the elementary row operations R2↔R3 and R3:=4R3. What is the value of det(B)?

a
 18
b
 −12
c
 −18
d
 24
e
 −24

solution.reasoning: Swapping two rows multiplies the determinant by −1, and multiplying one row by 4 multiplies it by 4. Therefore det(B)=−4·6=−24, option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is ${x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2}=40.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+6x)+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =40+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =49\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2} \\ (x-(-3))^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-3,0)$ and its radius is $7.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
$2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+4y) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+4)+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+4) & =\frac{13}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is ${x}^{2}-24x+{y}^{2}+6y=-137.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-24x+{y}^{2}+6y & =-137 \\ ({x}^{2}-24x)+({y}^{2}+6y) & =-137 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 12x+{12}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =-137+{12}^{2}+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 12x+{12}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-12)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ (x-12)^{2}+(y-(-3))^{2} & ={4}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(12,-3)$ and its radius is $4.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =2+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{3}{2}))}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x-2y=\frac{11}{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x-2y & =\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-x)+({y}^{2}-2y) & =\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot y+{1}^{2}) & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}+\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot y+{1}^{2}) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-1)}^{2} & ={2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ and its radius is $2.$

questions.raw_html:
5.Finding the Center and Radius of a Circle by Completing the Square with Fractions?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2−x−2y=114.

E
Tue, Oct 13th @ 12:29 PM|Elapsed: 0:15Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+6x)+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =40+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =49\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2} \\ (x-(-3))^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-3,0)$ and its radius is $7.$

Question 1
?

Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is x2+6x+y2=40.

a
center: (0,3), radius: 4
b
center: (0,−3), radius: 7
c
center: (−3,0), radius: 7
d
center: (3,3), radius: 2
e
center: (3,0), radius: 49
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+6x+y2=40(x2+6x)+y2=40(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=40+32(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=49

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+3)2+(y−0)2=72(x−(−3))2+(y−0)2=72.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−3,0) and its radius is 7.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+4y) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+4)+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+4) & =\frac{13}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

Question 2
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is 2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0.

a
center: (2,4), radius: 132
b
center: (−2,2), radius: 132
c
center: (−2,−2), radius: 132
d
center: (2,2), radius: 132
e
center: (2,−2), radius: 132
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0x2+y2−4x+4y=−32(x2−4x)+(y2+4y)=−32(x2−2⋅2x+22)+(y2+2⋅2y+22)=−32+22+22(x2−2⋅2x+4)+(y2+2⋅2x+4)=132

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−2)2+(y+2)2=132(x−2)2+(y−(−2))2=(132)2.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (2,−2) and its radius is 132.

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2−24x+y2+6y=−137(x2−24x)+(y2+6y)=−137(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=−137+122+32(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=16

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x−12)2+(y+3)2=42(x−12)2+(y−(−3))2=42.

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2+3x−y−2=0.

a

EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2+3x−y−2=0(x2+3x)+(y2−y)=2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=2+(32)2+(12)2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=92

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+32)2+(y−12)2=92(x−(−32))2+(y−12)2=(32)2

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−32,12) and its radius is 32.

Question 5
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2−x−2y=114.

a
center: (14,1), radius: 2
b
center: (12,1), radius: 4
c
center: (12,1), radius: 2
d
center: (−14,−1), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−1), radius: 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2−x−2y=114(x2−x)+(y2−2y)=114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=(12)2+12+114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=4

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−12)2+(y−1)2=22.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,1) and its radius is 2.

question.problem: Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is ${x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2}=40.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+6x)+{y}^{2} & =40 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =40+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2})+{y}^{2} & =49\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2} \\ (x-(-3))^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={7}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-3,0)$ and its radius is $7.$

center: (0,3), radius: 4
b
center: (0,−3), radius: 7
c
center: (−3,0), radius: 7
d
center: (3,3), radius: 2
e
center: (3,0), radius: 49
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+6x+y2=40(x2+6x)+y2=40(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=40+32(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=49

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+3)2+(y−0)2=72(x−(−3))2+(y−0)2=72.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−3,0) and its radius is 7.

Question 1
?

Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is x2+6x+y2=40.

a
center: (0,3), radius: 4
b
center: (0,−3), radius: 7
c
center: (−3,0), radius: 7
d
center: (3,3), radius: 2
e
center: (3,0), radius: 49
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+6x+y2=40(x2+6x)+y2=40(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=40+32(x2+2⋅3x+32)+y2=49

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+3)2+(y−0)2=72(x−(−3))2+(y−0)2=72.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−3,0) and its radius is 7.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
$2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3=0.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+4y) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+4)+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+4) & =\frac{13}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is 2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0.

a
center: (2,4), radius: 132
b
center: (−2,2), radius: 132
c
center: (−2,−2), radius: 132
d
center: (2,2), radius: 132
e
center: (2,−2), radius: 132
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0x2+y2−4x+4y=−32(x2−4x)+(y2+4y)=−32(x2−2⋅2x+22)+(y2+2⋅2y+22)=−32+22+22(x2−2⋅2x+4)+(y2+2⋅2x+4)=132

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−2)2+(y+2)2=132(x−2)2+(y−(−2))2=(132)2.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (2,−2) and its radius is 132.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+4y) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+4)+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+4) & =\frac{13}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is 2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0.

a
center: (2,4), radius: 132
b
center: (−2,2), radius: 132
c
center: (−2,−2), radius: 132
d
center: (2,2), radius: 132
e
center: (2,−2), radius: 132
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

2x2+2y2−8x+8y+3=0x2+y2−4x+4y=−32(x2−4x)+(y2+4y)=−32(x2−2⋅2x+22)+(y2+2⋅2y+22)=−32+22+22(x2−2⋅2x+4)+(y2+2⋅2x+4)=132

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−2)2+(y+2)2=132(x−2)2+(y−(−2))2=(132)2.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (2,−2) and its radius is 132.

solution.reasoning: Divide by 2 and complete the squares: x^2+y^2-4x+4y=-3/2, hence (x-2)^2+(y+2)^2=13/2. The center is (2,-2) and the radius is sqrt(13/2), matching choice e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
$2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3=0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-8x+8y+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-4x)+({y}^{2}+4y) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2y+{2}^{2}) & =-\frac{3}{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+4)+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+4) & =\frac{13}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{13}{2} \\ (x-2)^{2}+{(y-(-2))}^{2} & ={(\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(2,-2)$ and its radius is $\sqrt{\frac{13}{2}}.$

Question 3
?

Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is x2−24x+y2+6y=−137.

a
center: (3,12), radius: 4
b
center: (12,−3), radius: 4
c
center: (12,3), radius: 4
d
center: (−3,12), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−3), radius: 4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2−24x+y2+6y=−137(x2−24x)+(y2+6y)=−137(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=−137+122+32(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=16

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x−12)2+(y+3)2=42(x−12)2+(y−(−3))2=42.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,−3) and its radius is 4.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is x2−24x+y2+6y=−137.

a
center: (3,12), radius: 4
b
center: (12,−3), radius: 4
c
center: (12,3), radius: 4
d
center: (−3,12), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−3), radius: 4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2−24x+y2+6y=−137(x2−24x)+(y2+6y)=−137(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=−137+122+32(x2−2⋅12x+122)+(y2+2⋅3y+32)=16

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x−12)2+(y+3)2=42(x−12)2+(y−(−3))2=42.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,−3) and its radius is 4.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Find the center and radius of the circle whose equation is ${x}^{2}-24x+{y}^{2}+6y=-137.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-24x+{y}^{2}+6y & =-137 \\ ({x}^{2}-24x)+({y}^{2}+6y) & =-137 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 12x+{12}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =-137+{12}^{2}+{3}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 12x+{12}^{2})+({y}^{2}+2\cdot 3y+{3}^{2}) & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-12)^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & ={4}^{2} \\ (x-12)^{2}+(y-(-3))^{2} & ={4}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(12,-3)$ and its radius is $4.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2=0.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =2+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{3}{2}))}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2+3x−y−2=0.

a
center: (−32,12), radius: 92
b
center: (−32,12), radius: 32
c
center: (−92,32), radius: 32
d
center: (−92,32), radius: 92
e
center: (32,−12), radius: 32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2+3x−y−2=0(x2+3x)+(y2−y)=2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=2+(32)2+(12)2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=92

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+32)2+(y−12)2=92(x−(−32))2+(y−12)2=(32)2

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−32,12) and its radius is 32.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =2+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{3}{2}))}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2+3x−y−2=0.

a
center: (−32,12), radius: 92
b
center: (−32,12), radius: 32
c
center: (−92,32), radius: 32
d
center: (−92,32), radius: 92
e
center: (32,−12), radius: 32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2+3x−y−2=0(x2+3x)+(y2−y)=2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=2+(32)2+(12)2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=92

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+32)2+(y−12)2=92(x−(−32))2+(y−12)2=(32)2

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−32,12) and its radius is 32.

solution.reasoning: Completing the squares gives (x+3/2)^2+(y-1/2)^2=2+9/4+1/4=9/2. The center is (-3/2,1/2) and the radius is sqrt(9/2)=3/sqrt(2), matching choice b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2=0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+3x-y-2 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+3x)+({y}^{2}-y) & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =2+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}y+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{3}{2}))}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and its radius is $\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}.$

Question 4
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2+3x−y−2=0.

a
center: (−32,12), radius: 92
b
center: (−32,12), radius: 32
c
center: (−92,32), radius: 32
d
center: (−92,32), radius: 92
e
center: (32,−12), radius: 32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2+3x−y−2=0(x2+3x)+(y2−y)=2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=2+(32)2+(12)2(x2+2⋅32x+(32)2)+(y2−2⋅12y+(12)2)=92

Now, we can factor the perfect squares and get

(x+32)2+(y−12)2=92(x−(−32))2+(y−12)2=(32)2

Therefore, the circle is centered at (−32,12) and its radius is 32.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x-2y=\frac{11}{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-x-2y & =\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-x)+({y}^{2}-2y) & =\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot y+{1}^{2}) & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}+\frac{11}{4} \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2})+({y}^{2}-2\cdot y+{1}^{2}) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y-1)}^{2} & ={2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2−x−2y=114.

a
center: (14,1), radius: 2
b
center: (12,1), radius: 4
c
center: (12,1), radius: 2
d
center: (−14,−1), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−1), radius: 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2−x−2y=114(x2−x)+(y2−2y)=114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=(12)2+12+114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=4

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−12)2+(y−1)2=22.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,1) and its radius is 2.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2−x−2y=114.

a
center: (14,1), radius: 2
b
center: (12,1), radius: 4
c
center: (12,1), radius: 2
d
center: (−14,−1), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−1), radius: 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2−x−2y=114(x2−x)+(y2−2y)=114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=(12)2+12+114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=4

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−12)2+(y−1)2=22.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,1) and its radius is 2.

solution.reasoning: Completing the squares gives (x-1/2)^2+(y-1)^2=11/4+1/4+1=4. The center is (1/2,1) and the radius is 2, matching choice c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is x2+y2−x−2y=114.

a
center: (14,1), radius: 2
b
center: (12,1), radius: 4
c
center: (12,1), radius: 2
d
center: (−14,−1), radius: 4
e
center: (−12,−1), radius: 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group x and y terms and complete the squares.

x2+y2−x−2y=114(x2−x)+(y2−2y)=114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=(12)2+12+114(x2−2⋅12x+(12)2)+(y2−2⋅y+12)=4

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

(x−12)2+(y−1)2=22.

Therefore, the circle is centered at (12,1) and its radius is 2.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to C}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184928/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 2 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184928/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -23 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\},\,C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14184928/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & 8 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -11 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-11)-4\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ -4 & -11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}20 & -6 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 4 & 11\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
