questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$

$$

$$

Question 4
?

For the twice-differentiable function f:R2→R, we have the following data: f(1,1)=2,f′(1,1)=[31],f″(1,1)=[6330]

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[11] to approximate the value of f(0,2).

a
0
b
6
c
5
d
2
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defined by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have a=[11], and the following data:

f(a)=2,f′(a)=[31],f″(a)=[6330]

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

f(x)≈2+[31][x−1y−1]+12[x−1y−1]T[6330][x−1y−1]

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at x=[02], we obtain

f(0,2)≈2+[31][0−12−1]+12[0−12−1]T[6330][0−12−1]=2+[31][−11]+12[−11]T[6330][−11]=2+(−2)+12[−11][−3−3]=0+12(0)=0.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,2,0).$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The recorded submission was x-1 (option b), rather than my recommended 2x-3 (option a), so its Incorrect grade is consistent with the mathematics.

The two missing displacement entries are x-\pi/2, and f_{yy}=-x\cos y gives the missing Hessian entry -\pi/2. Their sum is 2x-3\pi/2, option e. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted value graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

At (1,2), f=e, the gradient is (3e,-e), and the Hessian is [[9e,-3e],[-3e,e]]. The six missing expressions sum to e+3e+(y-2)+(y-2)+9e-3e=2y+10e-4. This matches my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The recorded submission was x+y-3 (option b), so its Incorrect grade is consistent with the mathematics.

With displacement h=(-1,1), the linear term is -3+1=-2 and the quadratic term is (1/2)(6-6)=0. Thus the quadratic Taylor approximation is 2-2+0=0, option a. My earlier answer matches the submitted value graded Correct and the worked solution's final result.

The displacement is h=(-1,1,-1). The linear term is -4, and h^T Hh=-6, so the quadratic Taylor approximation is -1-4+(1/2)(-6)=-8, option c. This matches my earlier answer, the submitted value graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & ∗ \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2x+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

For the function f:R2→R, defined as

f(x,y)=x2+ex−y,

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[11] is given by

f(x,y)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12[∗y−1]T[3∗−11][∗y−1].

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.

a
2x−3
b
x−1
c
2−x
d
x
e
1−3x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defined by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have the following:

f′(x)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y],f″(x)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]

Calculating the first derivative, we have

f′(x)=[2x+ex−y−ex−y].

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

f″(x)=[2+ex−y−ex−y−ex−yex−y]f″(1,1)=[3−1−11]

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12[x−1y−1]T[3−1−11][x−1y−1].

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

(x−1)+(−1)+(x−1)=2x−3.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2x+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

question.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \operatorname{sin}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y & -x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-\frac{\pi }{2})+(-\frac{\pi }{2})+(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Question 2
?

For the function f:R2→R, defined as

f(x,y)=xcos⁡y+ysin⁡x,

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[π20] is given by

f(x,y)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12[∗y]T[000∗][∗y].

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.

a
x−π2
b
x−2π
c
2x
d
2x−π
e
2x−3π2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defined by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have the following:

f′(x)=[∂f∂x∂f∂y],f″(x)=[∂2f∂x2∂2f∂x∂y∂2f∂y∂x∂2f∂y2]

Calculating the first derivative, we have

f′(x)=[cos⁡y+ycos⁡xsin⁡x−xsin⁡y].

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

f″(x)=[−ysin⁡xcos⁡x−sin⁡ycos⁡x−sin⁡y−xcos⁡y]f″(π2,0)=[000−π2]

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12[x−π2y]T[000−π2][x−π2y].

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

(x−π2)+(−π2)+(x−π2)=2x−3π2.

solution.reasoning: Both missing displacement entries are x-\pi/2. Since f_{yy}(x,y)=-x\cos y, the missing Hessian entry at (\pi/2,0) is -\pi/2. Their sum is 2(x-\pi/2)-\pi/2=2x-3\pi/2, option e. No captured Math Academy answer evidence is provided.

question.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{3x-y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}∗ & -e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ ∗\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ ∗\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}].

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defened by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,2) & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3x-y} & -{e}^{3x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,2) & =[\begin{aligned}3e & -e\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x-y} & -3{e}^{3x-y} \\ -3{e}^{3x-y} & {e}^{3x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,2) & =[\begin{aligned}9e & -3e \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈e+[\begin{aligned}3e & -e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}9e & -3e \\ -3e & e\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-2\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$

$$

For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,2,0).$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

For the twice-differentiable function f:R3→R, we have the following data:

f(1,1,1)=−1,f′(1,1,1)=[202],f″(1,1,1)=[01−1101−110]

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a=[111] to approximate the value of f(0,2,0).

a
−2
b
1
c
−8
d
−6
e
−11
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose that the function f:Rn→R is defined by

f:[x1x2⋮xn]⟶z

and is twice differentiable at x=a. Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of f about a is given by

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+12(x−a)Tf″(a)(x−a),

where

f′(a)=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]|x=a

and

f″(a)=[∂2f∂x12∂2f∂x1∂x2⋯∂2f∂x1∂xn∂2f∂x2∂x1∂2f∂x22⋯∂2f∂x2∂xn⋮⋮⋮⋮∂2f∂xn∂x1∂2f∂xn∂x2⋯∂2f∂xn2]x=a

In this case, we have a=[111], and the following data:

f(a)=−1,f′(a)=[202],f″(a)=[01−1101−110]

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

f(x)≈−1+[202][x−1y−1z−1]+12[x−1y−1z−1]T[01−1101−110][x−1y−1z−1]

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at x=[020], we obtain

f(0,2,0)≈−1+[202][0−12−10−1]+12[0−12−10−1]T[01−1101−110][0−12−10−1]=−1+[202][−11−1]+12[−11−1]T[01−1101−110][−11−1]=−1+(−4)+12[−11−1][2−22]=−5+12(−6)=−8.

solution.reasoning: The displacement is h=(-1,1,-1). The linear term is (2,0,2)·h=-4. The quadratic term is (1/2)h^T Hh=h_1h_2-h_1h_3+h_2h_3=-1-1-1=-3. Thus the Taylor approximation is -1-4-3=-8, option c. No captured Math Academy answer evidence is provided.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,2,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2,0) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 0-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+(-4)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-5+\frac{1}{2}(-6) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$ A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(4t)={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t)={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of invertible matrices.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the properties of invertible matrices.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

where α1 and α0 are constants to be determined.

r((6i)t)=e(6i)tα1(6i)t+α0=cos⁡(6t)+isin⁡(6t)α0+6iα1t=cos⁡(6t)+isin⁡(6t)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(4t)={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t)={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{aligned}].
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the properties of invertible matrices.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

Question 5

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution x(t) can be written in the form x(t)=Φ(t)c for some constant vector c=[c1,c2]T is given below.

L1: Let x1(t) and x2(t) be the columns of Φ(t)

L2: x1(t) and x2(t) form a basis of solutions

L3: x(t) can be written as x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L4: Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L5: x(t)=Φ(t)c

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L3 follows from line L2 by
the definition of a basis
definition of matrix multiplication
the definition of a basis
integrating the given system
multiplying Φ(t) with its inverse
.

Line L4 follows from line L1 by the
definition of matrix multiplication
integrating the given system
multiplying Φ(t) with its inverse
definition of matrix multiplication
the definition of a basis
.

Line L5 follows from lines
L3 and L4
L1 and L2
L2 and L4
L1 and L3
L3 and L4
by the transitive property of equality.

Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Once x1(t) and x2(t) form a basis, every solution x(t) of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination
    x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Therefore, L3 follows from L2 by the definition of a basis.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L4. Since x1(t) and x2(t) are the columns of Φ(t), we can write Φ(t)=[||x1(t)x2(t)||]. Then by the definition of matrix multiplication, Φ(t)c=[||x1(t)x2(t)||][c1c2]=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Thus, L4 follows from L1 by the definition of matrix multiplication.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3 and L4. In L3 we have x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t), and in L4 we have Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives x(t)=Φ(t)c. Thus, L5 follows from L3 and L4.

question.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of invertible matrices.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the properties of invertible matrices.

question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of invertible matrices.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the properties of invertible matrices.

solution.reasoning: L1 names the columns of Φ. A fundamental matrix has linearly independent solution columns; uniqueness for the linear ODE ensures their independence at every t, giving L2. question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ states the independence of the columns of {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ by the {{field-3}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L2}.$ Line $\text{L2}$ states that the two columns of $Φ(t)$ are linearly independent, which is required of a fundamental matrix. Thus, $\text{L2}$ states independence of the columns of $Φ(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the $\text{properties of invertible matrices}.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ states the independence of the columns of {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ by the {{field-3}}.

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L2}.$ Line $\text{L2}$ states that the two columns of $Φ(t)$ are linearly independent, which is required of a fundamental matrix. Thus, $\text{L2}$ states independence of the columns of $Φ(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

question.html:
Question 5
?
Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution x(t) can be written in the form x(t)=Φ(t)c for some constant vector c=[c1,c2]T is given below.

L1: Let x1(t) and x2(t) be the columns of Φ(t)

L2: x1(t) and x2(t) form a basis of solutions

L3: x(t) can be written as x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L4: Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L5: x(t)=Φ(t)c

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L3 follows from line L2 by
the definition of a basis
definition of matrix multiplication
the definition of a basis
integrating the given system
multiplying Φ(t) with its inverse
.

Line L4 follows from line L1 by the
definition of matrix multiplication
integrating the given system
multiplying Φ(t) with its inverse
definition of matrix multiplication
the definition of a basis
.

Line L5 follows from lines
L3 and L4
L1 and L2
L2 and L4
L1 and L3
L3 and L4
by the transitive property of equality.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Once x1(t) and x2(t) form a basis, every solution x(t) of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination
    x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Therefore, L3 follows from L2 by the definition of a basis.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L4. Since x1(t) and x2(t) are the columns of Φ(t), we can write Φ(t)=[||x1(t)x2(t)||]. Then by the definition of matrix multiplication, Φ(t)c=[||x1(t)x2(t)||][c1c2]=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Thus, L4 follows from L1 by the definition of matrix multiplication.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3 and L4. In L3 we have x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t), and in L4 we have Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives x(t)=Φ(t)c. Thus, L5 follows from L3 and L4.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L4. Since x1(t) and x2(t) are the columns of Φ(t), we can write Φ(t)=[||x1(t)x2(t)||]. Then by the definition of matrix multiplication, Φ(t)c=[||x1(t)x2(t)||][c1c2]=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Thus, L4 follows from L1 by the definition of matrix multiplication.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3 and L4. In L3 we have x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t), and in L4 we have Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t). Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives x(t)=Φ(t)c. Thus, L5 follows from L3 and L4.

solution.reasoning: A basis spans the solution space, so L2 gives the constant-coefficient linear combination in L3. Matrix multiplication expresses Φ(t)c as the weighted sum of its columns, giving L4. L3 and L4 equal the same expression, so transitivity gives L5. These answers are mathematically certain, but no Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/ebe7727862c160f7684d07ce6474ce0d57a95b6963415a1c3fc651aa2f951fdb.png)

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{AB}∥\overset{⟷}{CD}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠AJI$ and $∠CIF$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AJI & =m∠CIF \\ 3x & ={75}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ={75}^{∘} \\ \frac{3x}{3} & =\frac{{75}^{∘}}{3} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} & ={25}^{∘} \\ x & ={25}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{AB}∥\overset{⟷}{CD}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠EIC$ and $∠IJA$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠EIC & =m∠IJA \\ 3x-{23}^{∘} & =2x+{31}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{23}^{∘} & =2x+{31}^{∘} \\ x-{23}^{∘} & ={31}^{∘} \\ x & ={54}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $r$, $s$ and $t$ in the above diagram are parallel, find $m∠1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider $∠2$ and $∠3$ in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/54294a339432476e3b426a8a4bbeca3e4a6f3d2bb3f6cd662f98dd0d5117a248.png)

Note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is ${97}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2={97}^{∘}.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠3$ and the angle whose measure is ${38}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠3={38}^{∘}.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/4042c15df28fd0d4055d95647fada0ad2ffc966a1561b7a021e1dfa62ed5d5ba.png)

The angles $∠1$, $∠2,$ and $∠3$ combined give a straight angle. So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2+m∠3 & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠1+{97}^{∘}+{38}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠1+{135}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠1 & ={45}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $s∥t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Consider $∠1$ and $∠2$ in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/fd9f8d0ecb9bf35fa0a3c8f478a2f25062d37013704d4e1b4e3b0de27c2b91cc.png)

Note that $∠1$ and the angle whose measure is $2x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠1=2x.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is $5x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2=5x.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/fe578ba5253792e812decdab76c76afd31e1d3e2f709bd202b1b0ecda5ef3fc4.png)

The angles $∠1$, $∠2,$ and the third angle whose measure is ${40}^{∘}$, combine to give a straight angle. So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x+5x+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x & ={140}^{∘} \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{{140}^{∘}}{7} \\ \frac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{7}} & ={20}^{∘} \\ x & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

tutorials.problem:
Consider the following pair of parallel lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD},$ and the transversal $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{EF}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/af403ef4827e840a49d5a3bde36561d22a508d262b3ad15b830812aefc306286.png)

 What is the value of $x?$

First, note that $\angle DIF$ and $\angle BJI$ are corresponding angles. Therefore, they are congruent and thus have the same measure. This means we can write down the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DIF & =m∠BJI \\ 3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we first subtract $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{20}^{∘} & =x+{10}^{∘} \\ 3x-{20}^{∘}-x & =x+{10}^{∘}-x \\ 2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $20^\circ$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘} \\ 2x-{20}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} & ={10}^{∘}+{20}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={30}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=15^\circ.$

Since the angles $\angle{CIF}$ and $\angle{AJI}$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠CIF & =m∠AJI \\ 5x+{10}^{∘} & ={110}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+{10}^{∘} & ={110}^{∘} \\ 5x & ={100}^{∘} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & =\frac{{100}^{∘}}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & ={20}^{∘} \\ x & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AJF & =m∠CIF \\ 9x-{10}^{∘} & =7x+{4}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}9x-{10}^{∘} & =7x+{4}^{∘} \\ 9x-7x & ={4}^{∘}+{10}^{∘} \\ 2x & ={14}^{∘} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{{14}^{∘}}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & ={7}^{∘} \\ x & ={7}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/259f366823da9de4543e0e245ec1186ac8f50e1a53616290e76271f9672a92f4.png)

Note that $∠1$ and the angle whose measure is $2x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠1=2x.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is $5x+{5}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2=5x+{5}^{∘}.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/10629276463e5cf33b4a0c5b0ba1237eec1201fe142e644628f0a6a96fa54c32.png)

The angles $∠1$, $∠2,$ and the third angle whose measure is ${70}^{∘}$, combine to give a straight angle. So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x+(5x+{5}^{∘})+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x+{75}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x & ={105}^{∘} \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{{105}^{∘}}{7} \\ \frac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{7}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

steps.title: Introduction
steps.html:
Introduction
?

A line that crosses two parallel lines is called a transversal. For example, the line in the diagram below is a transversal.

A pair of parallel lines with a transversal form a set of angles, shown below.

This set of eight angles can be grouped into two categories:

  • We have four pairs of vertical angles:
  • We also have four pairs of so-called corresponding angles:
    Corresponding pairs of angles are located in the same position as each other relative to the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal. Pairs of corresponding angles are congruent.

question.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠AJI$ and $∠CIF$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AJI & =m∠CIF \\ 3x & ={75}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ={75}^{∘} \\ \frac{3x}{3} & =\frac{{75}^{∘}}{3} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} & ={25}^{∘} \\ x & ={25}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠AJI$ and $∠CIF$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AJI & =m∠CIF \\ 3x & ={75}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & ={75}^{∘} \\ \frac{3x}{3} & =\frac{{75}^{∘}}{3} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}x}{\cancel{3}} & ={25}^{∘} \\ x & ={25}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solve for $x$ in the figure above given that $\overset{⟷}{AB}∥\overset{⟷}{CD}.$
question.worked_solution:
Since the angles $∠FID$ and $∠IJB$ are corresponding angles, they are congruent and therefore have the same measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠FID & =m∠IJB \\ {60}^{∘} & =8x-{4}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have an equation that we can solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{60}^{∘} & =8x-{4}^{∘} \\ {64}^{∘} & =8x \\ \frac{{64}^{∘}}{8} & =\frac{8x}{8} \\ {8}^{∘} & =\frac{\cancel{8}x}{\cancel{8}} \\ {8}^{∘} & =x \\ x & ={8}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider $∠1$ and $∠2$ in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/fd9f8d0ecb9bf35fa0a3c8f478a2f25062d37013704d4e1b4e3b0de27c2b91cc.png)

Note that $∠1$ and the angle whose measure is $2x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠1=2x.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is $5x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2=5x.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/fe578ba5253792e812decdab76c76afd31e1d3e2f709bd202b1b0ecda5ef3fc4.png)

The angles $∠1$, $∠2,$ and the third angle whose measure is ${40}^{∘}$, combine to give a straight angle. So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x+5x+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x+{40}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x & ={140}^{∘} \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{{140}^{∘}}{7} \\ \frac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{7}} & ={20}^{∘} \\ x & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/259f366823da9de4543e0e245ec1186ac8f50e1a53616290e76271f9672a92f4.png)

Note that $∠1$ and the angle whose measure is $2x$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠1=2x.
$$

Similarly, note that $∠2$ and the angle whose measure is $5x+{5}^{∘}$ are corresponding angles formed by the same transversal. Therefore, 

$$
m∠2=5x+{5}^{∘}.
$$

Let's add these measures to our diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14178066/assets/10629276463e5cf33b4a0c5b0ba1237eec1201fe142e644628f0a6a96fa54c32.png)

The angles $∠1$, $∠2,$ and the third angle whose measure is ${70}^{∘}$, combine to give a straight angle. So, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠1+m∠2+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 2x+(5x+{5}^{∘})+{70}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x+{75}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ 7x & ={105}^{∘} \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{{105}^{∘}}{7} \\ \frac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{7}} & ={15}^{∘} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{24}∼N(5,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=24$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=24,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{12}^{2}}{24}) \\  & ∼N(5,6).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{72}∼N(-1,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=72$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=72,\,\mu =-1,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-1,\frac{{12}^{2}}{72}) \\  & ∼N(-1,2).\end{aligned}
$$
