questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{36}∼N(4,{18}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $36$ from a normal population, calculate $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07).$ *Hint: Value tables of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\,0.02\,$$\,0.03\,$$\,0.04\,$
$\,-0.7\,$ $\,0.2358\,$ $\,0.2327\,$ $\,0.2296\,$
$\,-0.6\,$ $\,0.2676\,$ $\,0.2643\,$ $\,0.2611\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.3015\,$ $\,0.2981\,$ $\,0.2946\,$

$z$$\,0.02\,$$\,0.03\,$$\,0.04\,$
$\,-2.0\,$ $\,0.0217\,$ $\,0.0212\,$ $\,0.0207\,$
$\,-1.9\,$ $\,0.0274\,$ $\,0.0268\,$ $\,0.0262\,$
$\,-1.8\,$ $\,0.0344\,$ $\,0.0336\,$ $\,0.0329\,$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(4,\frac{{18}^{2}}{36}) \\  & ∼N(4,9).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =P(-2.07<\overset{―}{X}<2.07) \\  & =P(\frac{-2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}<Z<\frac{2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}) \\  & =P(-2.02<Z<-0.64) \\  & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.64) & =0.2611, \\ Φ(-2.02) & =0.0217.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02) \\  & =0.2611-0.0217 \\  & =0.2394.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{64}∼N(-14,{16}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $64$ from a normal population, calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86).$

*Hint: A value table of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.3015\,$ | $\,0.2981\,$ | $\,0.2946\,$ |
| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3372\,$ | $\,0.3336\,$ | $\,0.3300\,$ |
| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3745\,$ | $\,0.3707\,$ | $\,0.3669\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-14,\frac{{16}^{2}}{64}) \\  & ∼N(-14,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =P(Z>\frac{-14.86-(-14)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-0.43) & =1-P(Z\le -0.43) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.43)=0.3336.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =1-Φ(-0.43) \\  & =1-0.3336 \\  & =0.6664.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{40}∼N(12,{20}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $40$ from a normal population, calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}<11).$

*Hint: A value table of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3783\,$ | $\,0.3745\,$ | $\,0.3707\,$ |
| $\,-0.2\,$ | $\,0.4168\,$ | $\,0.4129\,$ | $\,0.4090\,$ |
| $\,-0.1\,$ | $\,0.4562\,$ | $\,0.4522\,$ | $\,0.4483\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(12,\frac{{20}^{2}}{40}) \\  & ∼N(12,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<11).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<11) & =P(Z<\frac{11-12}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.32) \\  & =Φ(-0.32)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.32)=0.3745.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<11) & =Φ(-0.32) \\  & =0.3745.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{16}∼N(-3,{8}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $16$ from a normal population, calculate $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$ *Hint: Value tables of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\,0.04\,$$\,0.05\,$$\,0.06\,$
$\,1.2\,$ $\,0.8925\,$ $\,0.8944\,$ $\,0.8962\,$
$\,1.3\,$ $\,0.9099\,$ $\,0.9115\,$ $\,0.9131\,$
$\,1.4\,$ $\,0.9251\,$ $\,0.9265\,$ $\,0.9279\,$

$z$$\,0.05\,$$\,0.06\,$$\,0.07\,$
$\,1.6\,$ $\,0.9505\,$ $\,0.9515\,$ $\,0.9525\,$
$\,1.7\,$ $\,0.9599\,$ $\,0.9608\,$ $\,0.9616\,$
$\,1.8\,$ $\,0.9678\,$ $\,0.9686\,$ $\,0.9693\,$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-3,\frac{{8}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(-3,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<0.5) \\  & =1-P(-0.5<\overset{―}{X}<0.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =1-P(1.25<Z<1.75) \\  & =1-(Φ(1.75)-Φ(1.25)) \\  & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & =0.8944, \\ Φ(1.75) & =0.9599.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75) \\  & =1+0.8944-0.9599 \\  & =0.9345.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
The concentration of solute of a certain chemical solution is normally distributed with a mean of $20\,\text{mg/ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{mg/ml}.$ Suppose $50$ bottles of this solution are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean concentration for this sample will be more than $19.9\,\text{mg/ml},$ but less than $20.1\,\text{mg/ml}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,-0.7\,$ $\,0.2420\,$ $\,0.2389\,$ $\,0.2358\,$
$\,-0.6\,$ $\,0.2743\,$ $\,0.2709\,$ $\,0.2676\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.3085\,$ $\,0.3050\,$ $\,0.3015\,$

$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,0.5\,$ $\,0.6915\,$ $\,0.6950\,$ $\,0.6985\,$
$\,0.6\,$ $\,0.7257\,$ $\,0.7291\,$ $\,0.7324\,$
$\,0.7\,$ $\,0.7580\,$ $\,0.7611\,$ $\,0.7642\,$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =20,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(20,\frac{{1}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(20,0.02).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =P(\frac{19.9-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}<Z<\frac{20.1-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}) \\  & =P(-0.71<Z<0.71) \\  & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.71) & =0.2389 \\ Φ(0.71) & =0.7611.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71) \\  & ≈0.7611-0.2389 \\  & =0.5222.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the probability that the mean weight for this sample will be more than $6.8\,\text{kg},$ but less than $7\,\text{kg}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =7,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=4.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & ∼N(7,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{7-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.4<Z<0) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-Φ(-0.4)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.4)=0.3446.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =0.5-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-0.3446 \\  & =0.1554.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
The scores in a standardized math test used for university admissions in a certain country are normally distributed with a mean of $57$ and a standard deviation of $16.$ Suppose $50$ test results are selected at random. What is the probability that the mean score for this sample will be less than $55?$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1469\,$ | $\,0.1446\,$ | $\,0.1423\,$ | $\,0.1401\,$ | $\,0.1379\,$ |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1711\,$ | $\,0.1685\,$ | $\,0.1660\,$ | $\,0.1635\,$ | $\,0.1611\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.1977\,$ | $\,0.1949\,$ | $\,0.1922\,$ | $\,0.1894\,$ | $\,0.1867\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =57$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =16,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(57,\frac{{16}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(57,5.12).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<55).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & =P(Z<\frac{55-57}{\sqrt{5.12}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.88) \\  & =Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.88)=0.1894.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & ≈Φ(-0.88) \\  & =0.1894.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
The systolic blood pressure of adults in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of $123.4\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $19.5\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Suppose $10$ adults are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean systolic blood pressure for this sample will be between $120\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and $125\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.04\,$ $\,0.05\,$ $\,0.06\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.2946\,$ $\,0.2912\,$ $\,0.2877\,$
$\,-0.4\,$ $\,0.3300\,$ $\,0.3264\,$ $\,0.3228\,$
$\,-0.3\,$ $\,0.3669\,$ $\,0.3632\,$ $\,0.3594\,$

$z$ $\,0.04\,$ $\,0.05\,$ $\,0.06\,$
$\,0.0\,$ $\,0.5160\,$ $\,0.5199\,$ $\,0.5239\,$
$\,0.1\,$ $\,0.5557\,$ $\,0.5596\,$ $\,0.5636\,$
$\,0.2\,$ $\,0.5948\,$ $\,0.5987\,$ $\,0.6026\,$
questions.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =123.4,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =19.5,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(123.4,\frac{{19.5}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(123.4,38.025).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =P(\frac{120-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}<Z<\frac{125-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}) \\  & =P(-0.55<Z<0.26) \\  & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.55) & =0.2912 \\ Φ(0.26) & =0.6026.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55) \\  & ≈0.6026-0.2912 \\  & =0.3114.\end{aligned}
$$

{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(15,\frac{{2}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(15,0.25).\end{aligned}

We're required to find $P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3).$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =P(\frac{14.7-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{15.3-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.6<Z<0.6) \\  & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6)\end{aligned}

$$

Example: 
                    Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{28} \sim N(8, 14^2)$ is a random sample of size $n = 28$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n = 28, \qquad
\mu = 8, \qquad
\sigma = 14.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(8,\frac{{14}^{2}}{28}) \\  & ∼N(8,7).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $X_1, X_2, \ldots,X_{100} \sim N(-4, 20^2)$ is a random sample of size $100$ from a normal population, calculate $P(-4.3 \lt \overline{X} \lt -3.9).$

*Hint: A value table of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\, 0.04 \,$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, -0.1 \,$ | $\, 0.4443 \,$ | $\, 0.4404 \,$ | $\, 0.4364 \,$ |
| $\, 0.0 \,$ | $\, 0.5160 \,$ | $\, 0.5199 \,$ | $\, 0.5239 \,$ |
| $\, 0.1 \,$ | $\, 0.5557 \,$ | $\, 0.5596 \,$ | $\, 0.5636 \,$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-4,\frac{{20}^{2}}{100}) \\  & ∼N(-4,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(-4.3 \lt \overline{X} \lt -3.9).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.3<\overset{―}{X}<-3.9) & =P(\frac{-4.3-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{-3.9-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.15<Z<0.05) \\  & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.05)=0.5199, \\ Φ(-0.15)=0.4404.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.15<Z<0.05) & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15) \\  & =0.5199-0.4404 \\  & =0.0795.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The diastolic blood pressure of adult men in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of $75\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $10\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Suppose $10$ men are selected at random. What is the probability that the mean diastolic blood pressure for this sample will be less than $70\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}?$

*Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. * 

| $z$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ | $\, 0.07 \,$ | $\, 0.08 \,$ | $\, 0.09 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, -1.5 \,$ | $\, 0.0606 \,$ | $\, 0.0594 \,$ | $\, 0.0582 \,$ | $\, 0.0571 \,$ | $\, 0.0559 \,$ |
| $\, -1.4 \,$ | $\, 0.0735 \,$ | $\, 0.0721 \,$ | $\, 0.0708 \,$ | $\, 0.0694 \,$ | $\, 0.0681 \,$ |
| $\, -1.3 \,$ | $\, 0.0885 \,$ | $\, 0.0869 \,$ | $\, 0.0853 \,$ | $\, 0.0838 \,$ | $\, 0.0823 \,$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu=75,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma = 10,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(75,\frac{{10}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(75,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P( \overline{X} \lt 70).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =P(Z<\frac{70-75}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.58) \\  & =Φ(-1.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.58) & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =Φ(-1.58) \\  & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ be a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2.$ In other words,   

$$
X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n} \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).
$$

In this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Recall the following:

- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
Y = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

is normally distributed.

- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y
$$

is normally distributed.

Also, we previously saw that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, i.e., 

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu,
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X24∼N(5,122) is a random sample of size n=24 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
N(25,6)
b
N(5,12)
c
N(25,12)
d
N(5,6)
e
N(5,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=24,μ=5,σ=12.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(5,12224)∼N(5,6).

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=64,\,\mu =-5,\,\sigma =16.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{{16}^{2}}{64}) \\  & ∼N(-5,4).\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Example: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sample Mean
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-4,\frac{{20}^{2}}{100}) \\  & ∼N(-4,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(-4.3 \lt \overline{X} \lt -3.9).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-4.3<\overset{―}{X}<-3.9) & =P(\frac{-4.3-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{-3.9-(-4)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.15<Z<0.05) \\  & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.05)=0.5199, \\ Φ(-0.15)=0.4404.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.15<Z<0.05) & =Φ(0.05)-Φ(-0.15) \\  & =0.5199-0.4404 \\  & =0.0795.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that X1,X2,…,X49∼N(7,142) is a random sample of size 49 from a normal population, calculate P(6.8<X―<7.5).

Hint: A value table of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(7,14249)∼N(7,4).

We're required to find P(6.8<X―<7.5).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring: P(6.8<X―<7.5)=P(6.8−74<Z<7.5−74)=P(−0.1<Z<0.25)=Φ(0.25)−Φ(−0.1)

From the table, we have Φ(0.25)=0.5987, and by the symmetry of the normal distribution, Φ(−0.1)=1−Φ(0.1)=1−0.5398=0.4602.

Therefore, P(6.8<X―<7.5)=Φ(0.25)−Φ(−0.1)=0.5987−0.4602=0.1385.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sample Mean
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(4,\frac{{18}^{2}}{36}) \\  & ∼N(4,9).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =P(-2.07<\overset{―}{X}<2.07) \\  & =P(\frac{-2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}<Z<\frac{2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}) \\  & =P(-2.02<Z<-0.64) \\  & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.64) & =0.2611, \\ Φ(-2.02) & =0.0217.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02) \\  & =0.2611-0.0217 \\  & =0.2394.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =P(Z>\frac{-14.86-(-14)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.43).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-0.43) & =1-P(Z\le -0.43) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.43).\end{aligned}

From the table, we have

$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =1-Φ(-0.43) \\  & =1-0.3336 \\  & =0.6664.\end{aligned}

If $X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i\leq n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overline{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu=75,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma = 10,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(75,\frac{{10}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(75,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P( \overline{X} \lt 70).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =P(Z<\frac{70-75}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.58) \\  & =Φ(-1.58)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.58) & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<70) & =Φ(-1.58) \\  & =0.0571.\end{aligned}
$$

The scores in a standardized math test used for university admissions in a certain country are normally distributed with a mean of 57 and a standard deviation of 16. Suppose 50 test results are selected at random. What is the probability that the mean score for this sample will be less than 55?

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

We're told that the population mean μ=57 the population standard deviation σ=16, and that the sample size n=50. Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is

X―∼N(57,16250)∼N(57,5.12).

We're required to find P(X―<55).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring:

P(X―<55)=P(Z<55−575.12)≈P(Z<−0.88)=Φ(−0.88)

Therefore,

P(X―<55)≈Φ(−0.88)=0.1894.

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =123.4,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =19.5,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(123.4,\frac{{19.5}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(123.4,38.025).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =P(\frac{120-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}<Z<\frac{125-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}) \\  & =P(-0.55<Z<0.26) \\  & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.55) & =0.2912 \\ Φ(0.26) & =0.6026.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55) \\  & ≈0.6026-0.2912 \\  & =0.3114.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{24}∼N(5,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=24$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=24,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{12}^{2}}{24}) \\  & ∼N(5,6).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X24∼N(5,122) is a random sample of size n=24 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
N(25,6)
b
N(5,12)
c
N(25,12)
d
N(5,6)
e
N(5,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=24,μ=5,σ=12.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(5,12224)∼N(5,6).

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X24∼N(5,122) is a random sample of size n=24 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
N(25,6)
b
N(5,12)
c
N(25,12)
d
N(5,6)
e
N(5,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=24,μ=5,σ=12.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(5,12224)∼N(5,6).
question.knowledge_point: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean

solution.reasoning: The sample mean is exactly normal because the population is normal. Its mean is 5 and its variance is 12^2/24=6, so \overline{X}\sim N(5,6), option d. The supplied example supports this variance convention, but no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{24}∼N(5,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=24$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=24,\,\mu =5,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{12}^{2}}{24}) \\  & ∼N(5,6).\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean
last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=64,\,\mu =-5,\,\sigma =16.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{{16}^{2}}{64}) \\  & ∼N(-5,4).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X64∼N(−5,162) is a random sample of size n=64 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
∼N(25,4)
b
∼N(25,16)
c
∼N(−5,2)
d
∼N(−5,16)
e
∼N(−5,4)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=64,μ=−5,σ=16.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(−5,16264)∼N(−5,4).
question.knowledge_point: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean

solution.reasoning: For an independent sample from a normal population, the sample mean is exactly normal with mean -5 and variance 16^2/64=4. Thus \overline{X}\sim N(-5,4), option e. The supplied example confirms the variance convention, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X72∼N(−1,122) is a random sample of size n=72 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
N(−1,6)
b
N(−1,4)
c
N(1,2)
d
N(1,6)
e
N(−1,2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=72,μ=−1,σ=12.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(−1,12272)∼N(−1,2).
question.knowledge_point: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean

solution.reasoning: The sample mean is exactly normal with mean -1 and variance 12^2/72=2, so \overline{X}\sim N(-1,2), option e. The supplied example supports the variance convention, but no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{72}∼N(-1,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $n=72$ from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=72,\,\mu =-1,\,\sigma =12.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-1,\frac{{12}^{2}}{72}) \\  & ∼N(-1,2).\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Stating the Distribution of the Sample Mean
last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=18,\,\mu =12,\,\sigma =6.
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(12,\frac{{6}^{2}}{18}) \\  & ∼N(12,2).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that X1,X2,…,X18∼N(12,62) is a random sample of size n=18 from a normal population, what is the distribution of the sample mean X―?

a
N(12,6)
b
N(6,2)
c
N(6,4)
d
N(12,2)
e
N(12,4)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

In our case, we have n=18,μ=12,σ=6.

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(12,6218)∼N(12,2).

solution.reasoning: The sample mean is exactly normal with mean 12 and variance 6^2/18=2, so \overline{X}\sim N(12,2), option d. The supplied example supports the variance convention, but no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

question.name: Question 6
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}

Given that X1,X2,…,X49∼N(7,142) is a random sample of size 49 from a normal population, calculate P(6.8<X―<7.5).

Hint: A value table of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z0.000.010.020.030.040.05
0.1 0.5398 0.5438 0.5478 0.5517 0.5557 0.5596
0.2 0.5793 0.5832 0.5871 0.5910 0.5948 0.5987

a
0.1385

EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(7,14249)∼N(7,4).

We're required to find P(6.8<X―<7.5).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring: P(6.8<X―<7.5)=P(6.8−74<Z<7.5−74)=P(−0.1<Z<0.25)=Φ(0.25)−Φ(−0.1)

From the table, we have Φ(0.25)=0.5987, and by the symmetry of the normal distribution, Φ(−0.1)=1−Φ(0.1)=1−0.5398=0.4602.

Therefore, P(6.8<X―<7.5)=Φ(0.25)−Φ(−0.1)=0.5987−0.4602=0.1385.

last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{14}^{2}}{49}) \\  & ∼N(7,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{7.5-7}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(-0.1<Z<0.25) \\  & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.25)=0.5987,\end{aligned}
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.1) & =1-Φ(0.1) \\  & =1-0.5398 \\  & =0.4602.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7.5) & =Φ(0.25)-Φ(-0.1) \\  & =0.5987-0.4602 \\  & =0.1385.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(4,\frac{{18}^{2}}{36}) \\  & ∼N(4,9).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =P(-2.07<\overset{―}{X}<2.07) \\  & =P(\frac{-2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}<Z<\frac{2.07-4}{\sqrt{9}}) \\  & =P(-2.02<Z<-0.64) \\  & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.64) & =0.2611, \\ Φ(-2.02) & =0.0217.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<2.07) & =Φ(-0.64)-Φ(-2.02) \\  & =0.2611-0.0217 \\  & =0.2394.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =P(Z>\frac{-14.86-(-14)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.43).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =1-Φ(-0.43) \\  & =1-0.3336 \\  & =0.6664.\end{aligned}

Given that X1,X2,…,X64∼N(−14,162) is a random sample of size 64 from a normal population, calculate P(X―>−14.86).

Hint: A value table of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z0.020.030.04

−0.3 0.3745 0.3707 0.3669

EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is X―∼N(−14,16264)∼N(−14,4).

We're required to find P(X―>−14.86).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring: P(X―>−14.86)=P(Z>−14.86−(−14)4)=P(Z>−0.43).

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have P(Z>−0.43)=1−P(Z≤−0.43)=1−Φ(−0.43).

From the table, we have Φ(−0.43)=0.3336.

Therefore, P(X―>−14.86)=1−Φ(−0.43)=1−0.3336=0.6664.

solution.reasoning: The sample mean has mean -14 and standard deviation 16/\sqrt{64}=2. The threshold standardizes to (-14.86+14)/2=-0.43. Therefore P(\overline{X}>-14.86)=1-\Phi(-0.43)=1-0.3336=0.6664, option b. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{64}∼N(-14,{16}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $64$ from a normal population, calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86).$

*Hint: A value table of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.3015\,$ | $\,0.2981\,$ | $\,0.2946\,$ |
| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3372\,$ | $\,0.3336\,$ | $\,0.3300\,$ |
| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3745\,$ | $\,0.3707\,$ | $\,0.3669\,$ |
feedback.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-14,\frac{{16}^{2}}{64}) \\  & ∼N(-14,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =P(Z>\frac{-14.86-(-14)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>-0.43) & =1-P(Z\le -0.43) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.43).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.43)=0.3336.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>-14.86) & =1-Φ(-0.43) \\  & =1-0.3336 \\  & =0.6664.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(12,\frac{{20}^{2}}{40}) \\  & ∼N(12,10).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<11) & =P(Z<\frac{11-12}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.32) \\  & =Φ(-0.32)\end{aligned}

If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(12,\frac{{20}^{2}}{40}) \\  & ∼N(12,10).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<11).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<11) & =P(Z<\frac{11-12}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.32) \\  & =Φ(-0.32)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.32)=0.3745.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<11) & =Φ(-0.32) \\  & =0.3745.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{16}∼N(-3,{8}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $16$ from a normal population, calculate $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$ *Hint: Value tables of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\,0.04\,$$\,0.05\,$$\,0.06\,$
$\,1.2\,$ $\,0.8925\,$ $\,0.8944\,$ $\,0.8962\,$
$\,1.3\,$ $\,0.9099\,$ $\,0.9115\,$ $\,0.9131\,$
$\,1.4\,$ $\,0.9251\,$ $\,0.9265\,$ $\,0.9279\,$

$z$$\,0.05\,$$\,0.06\,$$\,0.07\,$
$\,1.6\,$ $\,0.9505\,$ $\,0.9515\,$ $\,0.9525\,$
$\,1.7\,$ $\,0.9599\,$ $\,0.9608\,$ $\,0.9616\,$
$\,1.8\,$ $\,0.9678\,$ $\,0.9686\,$ $\,0.9693\,$
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-3,\frac{{8}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(-3,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<0.5) \\  & =1-P(-0.5<\overset{―}{X}<0.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =1-P(1.25<Z<1.75) \\  & =1-(Φ(1.75)-Φ(1.25)) \\  & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & =0.8944, \\ Φ(1.75) & =0.9599.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75) \\  & =1+0.8944-0.9599 \\  & =0.9345.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-3,\frac{{8}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(-3,4).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1-P(|\overset{―}{X}|<0.5) \\  & =1-P(-0.5<\overset{―}{X}<0.5) \\  & =1-P(\frac{-0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}<Z<\frac{0.5-(-3)}{\sqrt{4}}) \\  & =1-P(1.25<Z<1.75) \\  & =1-(Φ(1.75)-Φ(1.25)) \\  & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.25) & =0.8944, \\ Φ(1.75) & =0.9599.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|>0.5) & =1+Φ(1.25)-Φ(1.75) \\  & =1+0.8944-0.9599 \\  & =0.9345.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the probability that the mean weight for this sample will be more than $6.8\,\text{kg},$ but less than $7\,\text{kg}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =7,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=4.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & ∼N(7,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{7-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.4<Z<0) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-Φ(-0.4)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.4)=0.3446.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =0.5-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-0.3446 \\  & =0.1554.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

The weights of a particular breed of geese are normally distributed with a mean of 7kg and a standard deviation of 1kg. Suppose 4 geese are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean weight for this sample will be more than 6.8kg, but less than 7kg?

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z 0.00 0.01 0.02
−0.4 0.3446 0.3409 0.3372
−0.3 0.3821 0.3783 0.3745
−0.2 0.4207 0.4168 0.4129

z 0.00 0.01 0.02
−0.1 0.4602 0.4562 0.4522
0.0 0.5000 0.4960 0.4920
0.1 0.5398 0.5359 0.5319

a
0.0948
b
0.1554
c
0.1331
d
0.1628
e
0.1674
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

We're told that the population mean μ=7, the population standard deviation σ=1, and that the sample size n=4. Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is

X―∼N(7,124)∼N(7,0.25).

We're required to find P(6.8<X―<7).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring:

P(6.8<X―<7)=P(6.8−70.25<Z<7−70.25)=P(−0.4<Z<0)=Φ(0)−Φ(−0.4)=0.5−Φ(−0.4)

From the table, we have

Φ(−0.4)=0.3446.

Therefore,

P(6.8<X―<7)=0.5−Φ(−0.4)=0.5−0.3446=0.1554.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Probability Involving a Sample Mean in Context

solution.reasoning: The sample mean is normal with mean 7 and standard deviation 1/\sqrt{4}=0.5. Therefore P(6.8<\overline{X}<7)=P(-0.4<Z<0)=\Phi(0)-\Phi(-0.4)=0.5000-0.3446=0.1554, option b. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.problem:
The weights of a particular breed of geese are normally distributed with a mean of $7\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{kg}.$ Suppose $4$ geese are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean weight for this sample will be more than $6.8\,\text{kg},$ but less than $7\,\text{kg}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,-0.4\,$ $\,0.3446\,$ $\,0.3409\,$ $\,0.3372\,$
$\,-0.3\,$ $\,0.3821\,$ $\,0.3783\,$ $\,0.3745\,$
$\,-0.2\,$ $\,0.4207\,$ $\,0.4168\,$ $\,0.4129\,$

$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,-0.1\,$ $\,0.4602\,$ $\,0.4562\,$ $\,0.4522\,$
$\,0.0\,$ $\,0.5000\,$ $\,0.4960\,$ $\,0.4920\,$
$\,0.1\,$ $\,0.5398\,$ $\,0.5359\,$ $\,0.5319\,$
feedback.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =7,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=4.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(7,\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & ∼N(7,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =P(\frac{6.8-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{7-7}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.4<Z<0) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-Φ(-0.4)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.4)=0.3446.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6.8<\overset{―}{X}<7) & =0.5-Φ(-0.4) \\  & =0.5-0.3446 \\  & =0.1554.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
The scores in a standardized math test used for university admissions in a certain country are normally distributed with a mean of $57$ and a standard deviation of $16.$ Suppose $50$ test results are selected at random. What is the probability that the mean score for this sample will be less than $55?$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1469\,$ | $\,0.1446\,$ | $\,0.1423\,$ | $\,0.1401\,$ | $\,0.1379\,$ |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1711\,$ | $\,0.1685\,$ | $\,0.1660\,$ | $\,0.1635\,$ | $\,0.1611\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.1977\,$ | $\,0.1949\,$ | $\,0.1922\,$ | $\,0.1894\,$ | $\,0.1867\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =57$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =16,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(57,\frac{{16}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(57,5.12).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<55).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & =P(Z<\frac{55-57}{\sqrt{5.12}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.88) \\  & =Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.88)=0.1894.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & ≈Φ(-0.88) \\  & =0.1894.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =57$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =16,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(57,\frac{{16}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(57,5.12).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<55).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & =P(Z<\frac{55-57}{\sqrt{5.12}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.88) \\  & =Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.88)=0.1894.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<55) & ≈Φ(-0.88) \\  & =0.1894.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
The systolic blood pressure of adults in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of $123.4\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $19.5\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Suppose $10$ adults are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean systolic blood pressure for this sample will be between $120\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and $125\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.04\,$ $\,0.05\,$ $\,0.06\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.2946\,$ $\,0.2912\,$ $\,0.2877\,$
$\,-0.4\,$ $\,0.3300\,$ $\,0.3264\,$ $\,0.3228\,$
$\,-0.3\,$ $\,0.3669\,$ $\,0.3632\,$ $\,0.3594\,$

$z$ $\,0.04\,$ $\,0.05\,$ $\,0.06\,$
$\,0.0\,$ $\,0.5160\,$ $\,0.5199\,$ $\,0.5239\,$
$\,0.1\,$ $\,0.5557\,$ $\,0.5596\,$ $\,0.5636\,$
$\,0.2\,$ $\,0.5948\,$ $\,0.5987\,$ $\,0.6026\,$
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =123.4,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =19.5,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(123.4,\frac{{19.5}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(123.4,38.025).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =P(\frac{120-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}<Z<\frac{125-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}) \\  & =P(-0.55<Z<0.26) \\  & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.55) & =0.2912 \\ Φ(0.26) & =0.6026.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55) \\  & ≈0.6026-0.2912 \\  & =0.3114.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

The systolic blood pressure of adults in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of 123.4mmHg and a standard deviation of 19.5mmHg. Suppose 10 adults are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean systolic blood pressure for this sample will be between 120mmHg and 125mmHg?

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z 0.04 0.05 0.06
−0.5 0.2946 0.2912 0.2877
−0.4 0.3300 0.3264 0.3228
−0.3 0.3669 0.3632 0.3594

z 0.04 0.05 0.06
0.0 0.5160 0.5199 0.5239
0.1 0.5557 0.5596 0.5636
0.2 0.5948 0.5987 0.6026

a
0.2332
b
0.3114
c
0.3075
d
0.3149
e
0.1645
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

We're told that the population mean μ=123.4, the population standard deviation σ=19.5, and that the sample size n=10. Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is

X―∼N(123.4,19.5210)∼N(123.4,38.025).

We're required to find P(120<X―<125).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring:

P(120<X―<125)=P(120−123.438.025<Z<125−123.438.025)=P(−0.55<Z<0.26)=Φ(0.26)−Φ(−0.55)

From the table, we have

Φ(−0.55)=0.2912Φ(0.26)=0.6026.

Therefore,

P(120<X―<125)=Φ(0.26)−Φ(−0.55)≈0.6026−0.2912=0.3114.

last_observation.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =123.4,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =19.5,$ and that the sample size $n=10.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(123.4,\frac{{19.5}^{2}}{10}) \\  & ∼N(123.4,38.025).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =P(\frac{120-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}<Z<\frac{125-123.4}{\sqrt{38.025}}) \\  & =P(-0.55<Z<0.26) \\  & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.55) & =0.2912 \\ Φ(0.26) & =0.6026.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(120<\overset{―}{X}<125) & =Φ(0.26)-Φ(-0.55) \\  & ≈0.6026-0.2912 \\  & =0.3114.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The systolic blood pressure of adults in a given population is normally distributed with a mean of 123.4mmHg and a standard deviation of 19.5mmHg. Suppose 10 adults are randomly selected. What is the probability that the mean systolic blood pressure for this sample will be between 120mmHg and 125mmHg?

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z 0.04 0.05 0.06
−0.5 0.2946 0.2912 0.2877
−0.4 0.3300 0.3264 0.3228
−0.3 0.3669 0.3632 0.3594

z 0.04 0.05 0.06
0.0 0.5160 0.5199 0.5239
0.1 0.5557 0.5596 0.5636
0.2 0.5948 0.5987 0.6026

a
0.2332
b
0.3114
c
0.3075
d
0.3149
e
0.1645
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

We're told that the population mean μ=123.4, the population standard deviation σ=19.5, and that the sample size n=10. Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is

X―∼N(123.4,19.5210)∼N(123.4,38.025).

We're required to find P(120<X―<125).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring:

P(120<X―<125)=P(120−123.438.025<Z<125−123.438.025)=P(−0.55<Z<0.26)=Φ(0.26)−Φ(−0.55)

From the table, we have

Φ(−0.55)=0.2912Φ(0.26)=0.6026.

Therefore,

P(120<X―<125)=Φ(0.26)−Φ(−0.55)≈0.6026−0.2912=0.3114.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
The weights of sugar in different types of cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$ Suppose $16$ cookies are selected randomly. What is the probability that the mean amount of sugar per cookie for this sample will be more than $14.7\,\text{g},$ but less than $15.3\,\text{g}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,-0.7\,$ $\,0.2420\,$ $\,0.2389\,$ $\,0.2358\,$
$\,-0.6\,$ $\,0.2743\,$ $\,0.2709\,$ $\,0.2676\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.3085\,$ $\,0.3050\,$ $\,0.3015\,$

$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,0.5\,$ $\,0.6915\,$ $\,0.6950\,$ $\,0.6985\,$
$\,0.6\,$ $\,0.7257\,$ $\,0.7291\,$ $\,0.7324\,$
$\,0.7\,$ $\,0.7580\,$ $\,0.7611\,$ $\,0.7642\,$
question.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =15,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =2,$ and that the sample size $n=16.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(15,\frac{{2}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(15,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =P(\frac{14.7-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{15.3-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.6<Z<0.6) \\  & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.6) & ≈0.7257 \\ Φ(-0.6) & ≈0.2743.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6) \\  & ≈0.7257-0.2743 \\  & =0.4514.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The weights of sugar in different types of cookies are normally distributed with a mean of 15g and a standard deviation of 2g. Suppose 16 cookies are selected randomly. What is the probability that the mean amount of sugar per cookie for this sample will be more than 14.7g, but less than 15.3g?

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z 0.00 0.01 0.02
−0.7 0.2420 0.2389 0.2358
−0.6 0.2743 0.2709 0.2676
−0.5 0.3085 0.3050 0.3015

z 0.00 0.01 0.02
0.5 0.6915 0.6950 0.6985
0.6 0.7257 0.7291 0.7324
0.7 0.7580 0.7611 0.7642

a
0.4582
b
0.4648
c
0.5160
d
0.4514
e
0.3830
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If X1,X2,…,Xn is a random sample of size n from a normal population, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n, then the sample mean X― has the distribution X―∼N(μ,σ2n).

We're told that the population mean μ=15, the population standard deviation σ=2, and that the sample size n=16. Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean X― is

X―∼N(15,2216)∼N(15,0.25).

We're required to find P(14.7<X―<15.3).

First, we transform X into a standard normal random variable Z by z-scoring:

P(14.7<X―<15.3)=P(14.7−150.25<Z<15.3−150.25)=P(−0.6<Z<0.6)=Φ(0.6)−Φ(−0.6)

From the table, we have

Φ(0.6)≈0.7257Φ(−0.6)≈0.2743.

Therefore,

P(14.7<X―<15.3)=Φ(0.6)−Φ(−0.6)≈0.7257−0.2743=0.4514.

solution.reasoning: The sample mean is normal with mean 15 and standard deviation 2/\sqrt{16}=0.5. The bounds standardize to -0.6 and 0.6, so the probability is \Phi(0.6)-\Phi(-0.6)=0.7257-0.2743=0.4514, option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.problem:
The weights of sugar in different types of cookies are normally distributed with a mean of $15\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$ Suppose $16$ cookies are selected randomly. What is the probability that the mean amount of sugar per cookie for this sample will be more than $14.7\,\text{g},$ but less than $15.3\,\text{g}?$ *Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,-0.7\,$ $\,0.2420\,$ $\,0.2389\,$ $\,0.2358\,$
$\,-0.6\,$ $\,0.2743\,$ $\,0.2709\,$ $\,0.2676\,$
$\,-0.5\,$ $\,0.3085\,$ $\,0.3050\,$ $\,0.3015\,$

$z$ $\,0.00\,$ $\,0.01\,$ $\,0.02\,$
$\,0.5\,$ $\,0.6915\,$ $\,0.6950\,$ $\,0.6985\,$
$\,0.6\,$ $\,0.7257\,$ $\,0.7291\,$ $\,0.7324\,$
$\,0.7\,$ $\,0.7580\,$ $\,0.7611\,$ $\,0.7642\,$
feedback.worked_solution:
If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =15,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =2,$ and that the sample size $n=16.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(15,\frac{{2}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(15,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =P(\frac{14.7-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{15.3-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.6<Z<0.6) \\  & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.6) & ≈0.7257 \\ Φ(-0.6) & ≈0.2743.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6) \\  & ≈0.7257-0.2743 \\  & =0.4514.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/56b286d9b7c503c84891ebdf410797f715844eb8de344f71dc2fc652cbf3b5ef.png)

In the triangle above, what is the length of $\overset{―}{AC}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/85f119cdc6b7a80dd7cd4ea2a2a235e80723b7c2fe6837fa127beb8fd994d7ea.png)

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the shorter leg has length $x=3$ and the longer leg has length $\sqrt{3}x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}AC=\sqrt{3}x=\sqrt{3}\cdot 3=3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the length of the longer leg is $3\sqrt{3}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/4234a330c5f497e3eae5af5006b87197f6911114f8b104b9050223d08ae7d310.png)

In the triangle above, what is the length of the shorter leg?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/b8f2ba89d30a41072f635916eb07b394fd4bd83eb39181f13e852d1b776de5ee.png)

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $7\sqrt{3},$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7\sqrt{3} & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{7\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $7.$

questions.problem: What is the length of the side opposite the ${30}^{∘}$ angle in a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle if the side opposite the ${60}^{∘}$ angle has a length of $21?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/1f7084b210e13a9c2753c3ae8bfcc9302b109cc9584f589c6b8937536ae93682.png)

  

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $21,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}21 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\sqrt{3}}{3}=7\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $7\sqrt{3}.$

question.problem: What is the length of the side opposite the ${30}^{∘}$ angle in a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle if the side opposite the ${60}^{∘}$ angle has a length of $21?$
question.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/1f7084b210e13a9c2753c3ae8bfcc9302b109cc9584f589c6b8937536ae93682.png)

  

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $21,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}21 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\sqrt{3}}{3}=7\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $7\sqrt{3}.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: What is the length of the side opposite the ${30}^{∘}$ angle in a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle if the side opposite the ${60}^{∘}$ angle has a length of $21?$
question.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/1f7084b210e13a9c2753c3ae8bfcc9302b109cc9584f589c6b8937536ae93682.png)

  

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $21,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}21 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\sqrt{3}}{3}=7\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $7\sqrt{3}.$

Question 3
?

What is the length of the side opposite the 30∘ angle in a 30∘-60∘-90∘ triangle if the side opposite the 60∘ angle has a length of 21?

a
3
b
7
c
73
d
37
e
21
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's refer to our standard 30∘-60∘-90∘ triangle.

Since this is a 30∘-60∘-90∘ triangle, the length of the longer leg is 3 times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length 21, and the shorter leg has length x, so we have

21=3xx=213.

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

x=213=21⋅33⋅3=2133=73

So, the length of the shorter leg is 73.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: In an inverse variation, $y=\frac{1}{4}$ when $x=2.$ Find an equation that relates $x$ and $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

Next, we use the given data $y=\frac{1}{4}$ when $x=2$ to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{k}{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}\cdot 2 & =k \\ \frac{1}{2} & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our inverse variation equation is

$$
y=\frac{1}{2x}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: In an inverse variation, $y=9$ when $x=-4.$ Find an equation that relates $x$ and $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

Next, we use the given data $y=9$ when $x=-4$ to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =\frac{k}{(-4)} \\ 9\cdot (-4) & =k \\ -36 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our inverse variation equation is

$$
y=-\frac{36}{x}.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=3$ when $x=\frac{5}{3},$ find the value of $y$ when $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=3$ when $x=\frac{5}{3}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\frac{k}{(\frac{5}{3})} \\ 3\cdot \frac{5}{3} & =k \\ \frac{15}{3} & =k \\ 5 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y=\frac{5}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=2$ into this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=10$ when $x=\frac{3}{2},$ find the value of $y$ when $x=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=10$ when $x=\frac{3}{2}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =\frac{k}{(\frac{3}{2})} \\ 10\cdot (\frac{3}{2}) & =k \\ \frac{30}{2} & =k \\ 15 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y=\frac{15}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=3$ into this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{15}{3}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0.3$ | $20$ |
| $0.6$ | $10$ |
| $2$ | $3$ |

Given the table above, select the options that make the following statement true:

The variable $y$ is {{field-1}} proportional to $x,$ and the constant of variation is $k=$  {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
If $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ then we must have

$$
y=\frac{k}{x}.
$$

for some constant $k.$ Note that we can rewrite the above equation as follows.

$$
x\cdot y=k
$$

So, we will compute $x\cdot y=k$ for each row in the table. If we get the same value of $k$ for each row, then we can conclude that $y$ is inversely proportional to $x.$

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $x\cdot y=k$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0.3$ | $20$ | $0.3\cdot 20=6$ |
| $0.6$ | $10$ | $0.6\cdot 10=6$ |
| $2$ | $3$ | $2\cdot 3=6$ |

The results are all the same: in each row, we have $k=6.$ Therefore, we conclude:

The variable $y$ is $\text{inversely}$ proportional  to $x,$ and the constant of variation is $k=6.$

Example: 
                    Finding an Inverse Variation Equation Given One Data Point
canonical_examples.problem: In an inverse variation, $y=5$ when $x=8.$ Find an equation that relates $x$ and $y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\dfrac{k}{x}.
$$

Next, we use the data $y=5$ when $x=8$ to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =\frac{k}{8} \\ 5\cdot 8 & =k \\ 40 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our inverse variation equation is

$$
y = \dfrac{40}{x}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Second Data Point Given Another Data Point
canonical_examples.problem: If $y$ varies inversely with $x$ and $y=15$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{5}$, find the value of $y$ when $x=3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=\dfrac{k}{x}.
$$

We are told that $y=15$ when $x=\dfrac{3}{5}.$ We substitute this data into the equation to find $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =\frac{k}{(\frac{3}{5})} \\ 15\cdot (\frac{3}{5}) & =k \\ \frac{45}{5} & =k \\ 9 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the inverse variation is given by 

$$
y = \dfrac{9}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the value of $x=3$ into this equation gives

$$
y=\dfrac{9}{3} = 3.
$$

Consider the table above. Which of the following statements is true?

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ then we must have

$$
y = \dfrac{k}{x},

for some constant $k.$ Note that we can rewrite the above equation as follows.

$$
x \cdot y = k

So, we will compute $x\cdot y = k$ for each row in the table. If we get the same value of $k$ for each row, then we can conclude that $y$ is inversely proportional to $x.$

| $2$ | $4$ | $2\cdot 4=8$ |
| $4$ | $2$ | $4\cdot 2=8$ |

The results are all the same: in each row, we have $k=8.$ Therefore, $y$ varies inversely with $x,$ and the constant of variation is $k=8.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we're making a juice drink with a fixed amount of pure orange and the rest water. 

The more water that we add, the less that we'll be able to taste the orange. 

More precisely, the concentration of pure orange $y$ (in grams per liter) varies **inversely** with the volume $x$ (in liters) of water added. We can express this idea using an **inverse variation equation** as follows:

$$
y= \dfrac{k}{x}
$$

The constant $k$ is called the **constant of variation** or **constant of proportionality.**

Notice that:

- If $x$ is small (i.e., there is not much water), then $y$ is large (i.e., there is a high concentration of orange).

- If $x$ is large (i.e., there is lots of water), then $y$ is small (i.e., there is a low concentration of orange).

To find the constant of variation $k$, we need to plug in some data. 

For example, suppose we know that the concentration is $y = 200\, \textrm{g/L}$ when $x = 4\,\textrm L$ of water has been added. Plugging this into our relationship and solving for $k,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{k}{x} \\ 200 & =\frac{k}{4} \\ 200\cdot 4 & =k \\ 800 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the relationship between $y$ and $x$ is

$$
y = \dfrac {800} x.
$$

Finally, notice that we can rewrite the above relationship as

$$
xy = 800.
$$
